title: Right to Equality
definition: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
simplifiedExplanation: Every person in India must be treated equally by law. Reasonable classification allowed. "arbitrariness" test from E.P. Royappa case.
punishment: Not applicable. Violation challenged under Article 32 or 226.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India (citizens and non-citizens)
realWorldExample: Rahul was denied a government hospital bed for an unofficial VIP wing. Court held government hospitals cannot create VIP wings denying equal access.

importantCases.caseName: E.P. Royappa vs State of TN
importantCases.summary: Equality means absence of arbitrariness.

importantCases.caseName: Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Articles 14,19,21 are trinity. Procedure must be fair.

importantCases.caseName: Indra Sawhney vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Upheld OBC reservations with 50% ceiling and creamy layer.

loopholes.description: Allows different treatment if intelligible differentia + rational nexus.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Governments create classifications appearing reasonable.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Argue both tests must be satisfied.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge as over-inclusive/under-inclusive.

loopholes.description: Arbitrariness test is subjective � varies by judge.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Actions defended as policy decisions.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show no intelligible justification.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply proportionality analysis.

title: Prohibition of Discrimination
definition: State shall not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. No disability in access to shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, roads, public places.
simplifiedExplanation: State cannot discriminate on 5 grounds. Special provisions for women, children, SC/ST/OBC in education allowed. Private establishments open to public also cannot discriminate.
punishment: Violation challenged through writs. SC/ST Atrocities Act for caste discrimination.
whoItAppliesTo: All citizens against State; all persons for public places
realWorldExample: Private restaurant refused entry to Dalit students. Court held even private establishments open to public cannot discriminate based on caste.

importantCases.caseName: Champakam Dorairajan
importantCases.summary: Struck down caste-based reservations in education. Led to First Amendment adding Article 15(4).

loopholes.description: Word "only" means discrimination prohibited only if SOLELY on listed grounds.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Discriminators argue additional factors beyond caste/religion.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Courts interpret that if caste is significant factor, Article 15 violated.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show prohibited ground was dominant reason.

title: Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
definition: Equality of opportunity for all citizens in government employment. No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence.
simplifiedExplanation: Equal opportunity in government jobs. Reservations for SC/ST/OBC allowed. "Creamy layer" excluded from OBC reservation.
punishment: Not applicable. Violation challenged through writ petitions.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens applying for government employment
realWorldExample: State govt announced 100% local reservation. SC struck down as violating Article 16(2) discrimination based on residence.

importantCases.caseName: Indra Sawhney vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Upheld 27% OBC reservation with creamy layer exclusion. Reservation cannot exceed 50%.

importantCases.caseName: M. Nagaraj vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Upheld SC/ST promotion reservation with conditions: backwardness, inadequate representation, efficiency.

loopholes.description: OBC creamy layer threshold debated. Should it apply to SC/ST?
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Advanced OBC families claim reservation benefits despite prosperity.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Regular threshold revision. Burden on candidate to prove non-creamy layer.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Courts: creamy layer applies to OBC, debated for SC/ST.

scenarioTags: denied government job due to caste

title: Abolition of Untouchability
definition: "Untouchability" is abolished. Its practice in any form is forbidden and punishable.
simplifiedExplanation: Untouchability completely abolished. Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 and SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989 implement this.
punishment: PCR Act: up to 6 months. SC/ST Atrocities Act: stringent minimum 5 years.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons
realWorldExample: Dalits denied use of village well and temple entry. Offenders charged under SC/ST Atrocities Act.

importantCases.caseName: Appa Balu Ingale
importantCases.summary: Article 17 is constitutional commitment to eradicate caste discrimination. PCR Act interpreted liberally.

loopholes.description: High acquittal rate due to delay, pressure to settle.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Accused claim fabricated caste angle or personal dispute.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Examine context, past conduct. Independent witnesses strengthen case.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Prove accused knew victim SC/ST status and acted on that ground.

title: Protection of Six Freedoms
definition: All citizens have right to: (a) speech/expression; (b) peaceful assembly; (c) associations/unions; (d) free movement; (e) residence/settlement; (f) profession/occupation/trade/business. Subject to reasonable restrictions.
simplifiedExplanation: Six fundamental freedoms for citizens. Government can impose reasonable restrictions for sovereignty, security, public order, decency, morality.
punishment: Not penal provision. Violations challenged through writ petitions.
whoItAppliesTo: Indian citizens only
realWorldExample: Journalist criticized government flood handling. Police filed FIR. Court struck down FIR � criticism of government is protected speech.

importantCases.caseName: Shreya Singhal vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Section 66A IT Act struck down as vague and chilling free speech.

importantCases.caseName: Romesh Thappar vs State of Madras
importantCases.summary: Press freedom is part of Article 19(1)(a).

loopholes.description: What is "reasonable" varies. Governments impose internet shutdowns, ban protests.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Governments argue "public order" to restrict speech.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Test: proportionate, least restrictive means, direct nexus.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply proportionality test.

title: Protection re Conviction for Offences
definition: (1) No ex-post-facto law. (2) No double jeopardy. (3) No self-incrimination.
simplifiedExplanation: Three protections: no punishment for act that was not crime when done, no trial twice for same offence, no forced self-testimony. Right to silence.
punishment: Not penal provision. Protections against unfair prosecution.
whoItAppliesTo: All accused persons
realWorldExample: Ravi acquitted of theft. New CCTV found � tried again. Court held double jeopardy � once acquitted, cannot be retried.

importantCases.caseName: Nandini Satpathy vs P.L. Dani
importantCases.summary: Right against self-incrimination extends to police interrogation.

importantCases.caseName: Selvi vs State of Karnataka
importantCases.summary: Narco-analysis, polygraph, brain-mapping violate Article 20(3) without consent.

loopholes.description: If same act constitutes different offences, separate trials allowed.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Prosecution charges multiple offences for same act.
loopholes.howToOvercome: If offences from same facts with same ingredients, it is double jeopardy.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply Maqbool Hussain test.

title: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
definition: No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
simplifiedExplanation: Most powerful fundamental right. Includes dignity, privacy, livelihood, health, education, shelter, clean environment. Procedure must be fair, just, reasonable.
punishment: Not a penal provision. Violating laws struck down by courts.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India � citizens and non-citizens
realWorldExample: Homeless people in Delhi forcibly evicted without alternative shelter during winter. SC held right to shelter is part of Article 21.

importantCases.caseName: K.S. Puttaswamy vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: 9-judge bench: privacy is fundamental right under Article 21.

importantCases.caseName: Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Article 21 procedure must be fair, just, reasonable. Connected Articles 14,19,21.

importantCases.caseName: Olga Tellis vs B.M.C.
importantCases.summary: Right to livelihood is part of right to life.

importantCases.caseName: Vishaka vs State of Rajasthan
importantCases.summary: Workplace sexual harassment guidelines under Article 21.

loopholes.description: Post-Maneka requires fair procedure but government passes unfair laws like UAPA.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Laws allow detention without trial.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Argue procedure must satisfy fairness test.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Invoke Maneka Gandhi doctrine.

loopholes.description: How far does Article 21 extend? Right to die? Internet?
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Creative expansion of rights.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Courts use core and periphery test.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Argue from constitutional morality.

writ.writExample: Family files HC when police detain illegally.

title: Protection Against Arrest and Detention
definition: (1) Right to know grounds of arrest. (2) Right to consult lawyer. (3) Produced before magistrate within 24 hours. Exceptions: enemy aliens and preventive detention.
simplifiedExplanation: Arrest rights: know why arrested, lawyer, magistrate in 24 hrs. Preventive detention has separate safeguards: grounds within 5 days, Advisory Board review.
punishment: Police violating rights face departmental action.
whoItAppliesTo: All arrested persons (except preventive detention and enemy aliens)
realWorldExample: Sameer arrested at 10 PM, produced at 6 PM next day. Court ordered release � violated 24-hour rule.

importantCases.caseName: D.K. Basu vs State of WB
importantCases.summary: 11 mandatory arrest requirements: memo, family info, medical exam, no torture, magistrate within 24 hrs.

importantCases.caseName: A.K. Roy vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Preventive detention safeguards must be strictly followed.

loopholes.description: Article 22(3) excludes preventive detention from arrest safeguards.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Government detains without 24-hr magistrate production using UAPA/NSA.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Safeguards under 22(4)-(7) must be strictly followed: grounds within 5 days, review board.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge: grounds not communicated, mala fides.

title: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Writs)
definition: Right to move SC for enforcement of Part III rights. SC can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari.
simplifiedExplanation: Ambedkar: "heart and soul of Constitution". Direct SC access for FR violations. Five writs available.
punishment: Not applicable. You can enforce fundamental rights.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person whose FRs are violated
realWorldExample: Amit illegally detained. Family filed Habeas Corpus under Article 32. SC ordered police to produce Amit.

importantCases.caseName: Bandhua Mukti Morcha vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Relaxed locus standi � any public-spirited person can file PIL.

importantCases.caseName: ADM Jabalpur vs Shivkant Shukla
importantCases.summary: Majority: Article 32 can be suspended. Justice Khanna dissented: right to life cannot be suspended.

loopholes.description: Article 359 allows suspension of Article 32 during Emergency.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: 1975 Emergency saw Article 32 suspended.
loopholes.howToOvercome: 44th Amendment protects Articles 20,21 from suspension.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Cite 44th Amendment and ADM Jabalpur dissent.

writ.writDescription: SC can issue all five writs.
writ.writExample: NGO files PIL for clean air under Article 21.

title: Uniform Civil Code
definition: State shall endeavour to secure Uniform Civil Code for all citizens throughout India.
simplifiedExplanation: Government should create common personal laws for all citizens regardless of religion. Currently different laws for Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis. Non-enforceable Directive Principle.
punishment: Not applicable � Directive Principle, not legally enforceable.
whoItAppliesTo: Directive to the State (government and legislature)
realWorldExample: Goa is only Indian state with UCC � Portuguese Civil Code 1867 applies to all Goans regardless of religion.

importantCases.caseName: Shah Bano vs M.A. Khan
importantCases.summary: Granted maintenance to 62-year-old Muslim woman. Called for UCC.

importantCases.caseName: Sarla Mudgal vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Hindu men converting to Islam for bigamy. Condemned and urged UCC.
importantCases.significance: Highlighted forum shopping in personal laws.

loopholes.description: Article 44 cannot be enforced by courts. Government has no legal obligation.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Governments avoid UCC citing political sensitivity.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Courts repeatedly directed government to consider UCC.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Invoke with Article 14 to argue inequality.

scenarioTags: different marriage laws for different religions

title: Fundamental Duties
definition: Eleven duties: (a) abide by Constitution; (b) cherish ideals; (c) uphold sovereignty; (d) defend country; (e) promote harmony; (f) value culture; (g) protect environment; (h) scientific temper; (i) safeguard public property; (j) strive for excellence; (k) educate children 6-14.
simplifiedExplanation: 11 moral obligations added by 42nd Amendment (1976). Not legally enforceable but used by courts for interpretation.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens
realWorldExample: SC cited Article 51A(g) (duty to protect environment) to justify stricter pollution control standards for factories.

importantCases.caseName: AIIMS Students Union vs AIIMS
importantCases.summary: Fundamental Duties guide interpretation of ambiguous laws.

loopholes.description: Duties not enforceable. No mechanism for non-compliance.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Citizens ignore duties without consequence.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Parliament can enact laws giving effect to duties.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Use duties as interpretive tools with rights.

title: Presidential Pardon Power
definition: President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, commute sentences for: (a) Court Martial; (b) Union law offences; (c) Death sentences.
simplifiedExplanation: President can pardon, reduce or commute sentences. Particularly important for death penalty cases. Governor under Article 161 cannot pardon death sentences.
whoItAppliesTo: President of India, for convicted persons
realWorldExample: Rajiv Gandhi assassination case: 4 death convicts' mercy petitions pending for over a decade. President rejected; convicts executed in 2022.

importantCases.caseName: Kehar Singh vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: President must decide mercy petitions on merits. Court can review on limited grounds.

importantCases.caseName: Shatrughan Chauhan vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Delay over 2 years in mercy petition entitles commutation to life.

loopholes.description: No time limit for President to decide mercy petitions.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Government uses delay tactic � keeps petitions pending for years.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Delay exceeding 2 years entitles commutation per Shatrughan Chauhan.
loopholes.courtStrategy: File writ citing delay violates Article 21.

title: Attorney-General for India
definition: President appoints a person qualified as SC judge to be Attorney-General. AG advises government on legal matters, has right of audience in all courts.
simplifiedExplanation: Highest law officer of India. Gives legal advice, represents government in courts, can speak in Parliament but cannot vote. Removable by President at any time.
whoItAppliesTo: Attorney General, Government of India
realWorldExample: AG appears in SC representing Union of India on constitutional issues like Aadhaar validity, demonetization, Article 370 abrogation.

importantCases.caseName: Union of India vs ADR
importantCases.summary: AG argued for government on electoral reforms. Court directed candidates to disclose criminal antecedents.
importantCases.significance: Showed AG's role defending government policy.

loopholes.description: AG holds office during President's pleasure � political appointee.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: AG may tailor opinions to suit government agenda.
loopholes.howToOvercome: AG should recuse if conflict. Office demands independence.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Independence depends on convention and personal integrity.

title: Parliamentary Privileges
definition: (1) Freedom of speech in Parliament. (2) MPs not liable for anything said or voted in Parliament. (3) Other privileges defined by Parliament.
simplifiedExplanation: MPs have absolute privilege for speech in Parliament � cannot be sued for defamation. Does NOT extend to repeating outside Parliament.
punishment: Not applicable. Parliament can punish own members for breach of privilege.
whoItAppliesTo: Members of Parliament
realWorldExample: MP alleged corruption in Parliament. Minister threatened defamation. MP protected inside Parliament. When MP repeated at press conference, defamation applied.

importantCases.caseName: K.A. Mathialagan vs P. Srinivasan
importantCases.summary: Parliamentary privilege absolute for proceedings in House, not outside.

loopholes.description: MPs make false allegations hiding behind absolute privilege. No remedy for harmed person.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: False allegations inside Parliament for political gain.
loopholes.howToOvercome: File complaint with Speaker/Chairperson. MP can be asked to apologize.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Some courts suggest malicious false statements not covered.

title: Definition of Money Bills
definition: A Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with: tax imposition/abolition/regulation, government borrowing, Consolidated Fund custody, appropriation, expenditure charged on Consolidated Fund.
simplifiedExplanation: Only Lok Sabha can introduce Money Bills. Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days. Definition has been controversial — some bills passed as Money Bills to bypass Rajya Sabha.
whoItAppliesTo: Parliament
realWorldExample: Aadhaar Act was passed as Money Bill in Lok Sabha, bypassing Rajya Sabha. Challenged in SC — constitutional validity debated.

importantCases.caseName: Raja Ram Pal vs Lok Sabha
importantCases.summary: SC can review Money Bill certification by Speaker.
importantCases.significance: Judicial review of Money Bill certification.

loopholes.description: Government passes non-Money Bills as Money Bills to avoid Rajya Sabha approval.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Aadhaar Act, Finance Acts passed as Money Bills.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Challenge certification as fraudulent if bill contains non-money matters.
loopholes.courtStrategy: SC can examine whether bill is genuinely Money Bill.

title: Ordinance Power of President
definition: President can promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session if circumstances require immediate action. Same force as laws. Must be approved by Parliament within 6 weeks of reassembly.
simplifiedExplanation: President can make temporary laws (ordinances) when Parliament is not in session. Has same effect as Act of Parliament. Must be approved within 6 weeks. Can be withdrawn. Used extensively by governments.
whoItAppliesTo: President, Parliament
realWorldExample: Government promulgated 30+ ordinances during COVID-19 pandemic including amendments to labour laws. Opposition criticized excessive use of ordinance power.

importantCases.caseName: D.C. Wadhwa vs State of Bihar
importantCases.summary: Re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative approval is unconstitutional.

loopholes.description: Governments re-promulgate ordinances repeatedly to bypass legislature.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Bihar government re-promulgated 256 ordinances.
loopholes.howToOvercome: SC held re-promulgation without legislative approval is fraud on Constitution.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Cite D.C. Wadhwa — re-promulgation is unconstitutional.

title: Special Leave Petition (SLP)
definition: SC may grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order of any court or tribunal in India.
simplifiedExplanation: SC's discretionary power to hear appeals from any court/tribunal. NOT a right — purely discretionary. Used for important constitutional/legal questions. Can be against HC, tribunals, military courts.
whoItAppliesTo: Any party aggrieved by court/tribunal decision
realWorldExample: After losing in HC, a party can file SLP in SC. SC may refuse SLP without giving reasons. If granted, SC hears full appeal.

importantCases.caseName: Pritam Singh vs State of UP
importantCases.summary: SLP should be granted only if substantial question of law or grave injustice.

loopholes.description: SC can refuse SLP without reasons. Creates uncertainty.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: SC refuses most SLPs (90%+). No remedy against refusal.
loopholes.howToOvercome: No solution — purely discretionary.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Evolves through practice directions.

title: Law Declared by SC is Binding
definition: Law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
simplifiedExplanation: SC decisions are binding precedent on ALL courts in India — Supreme Court, High Courts, subordinate courts. Doctrine of stare decisis. Only SC can overrule its own decisions.
whoItAppliesTo: All courts in India
realWorldExample: SC held privacy is fundamental right in Puttaswamy (2017). All HCs and lower courts must follow this in privacy-related cases.

importantCases.caseName: CIT vs Sun Engineering Works
importantCases.summary: Only ratio decidendi (reason for decision) is binding, not obiter dicta (incidental remarks).

loopholes.description: Only ratio decidendi is binding. Obiter dicta is not. Difficult to distinguish sometimes.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Parties argue SC observations were obiter, not binding.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Court examines if observation was necessary for the decision (ratio) or incidental (obiter).
loopholes.courtStrategy: Only the core reasoning is binding.

title: SC Power to Do Complete Justice
definition: SC in exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.
simplifiedExplanation: SC can pass ANY order to ensure complete justice — even beyond statutory law. Used in high-profile cases to fill legal gaps, grant reliefs Parliament hasn't provided.
whoItAppliesTo: Supreme Court
realWorldExample: SC used Article 142 to dissolve a marriage where it was irretrievably broken, even though irretrievable breakdown was not a statutory ground for divorce under Hindu Marriage Act.

importantCases.caseName: Union Carbide vs Union of India (Bhopal)
importantCases.summary: Used Article 142 to settle Bhopal gas tragedy claims. SC can override statutory law for complete justice.
importantCases.significance: Complete justice power vs statutory law.

loopholes.description: Article 142 cannot override statutory law per SC but boundary is unclear.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: SC sometimes overrides clear statutory provisions citing "complete justice".
loopholes.howToOvercome: SC must exercise power within constitutional framework. Cannot override fundamental rights.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Judicial restraint required — otherwise becomes super-legislature.

title: Power of High Courts to Issue Writs
definition: Every High Court shall have power throughout its jurisdiction to issue to any person or authority directions, orders or writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto for enforcement of Part III rights and for any other purpose.
simplifiedExplanation: HC can issue 5 writs for both fundamental rights AND other legal rights. Wider than Article 32 which only covers FRs. Most powerful remedy available to citizens.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person approaching High Court for violation of rights
realWorldExample: Police refused to register a complaint. Victim filed Mandamus in HC directing police to register FIR. HC ordered police to register it.

importantCases.caseName: T.C. Basappa vs T. Nagappa
importantCases.summary: HC writ jurisdiction is plenary. HC can issue writs even when alternative remedy exists.
importantCases.significance: HC writ power vs alternative remedy.

loopholes.description: Courts often refuse writ if alternative remedy (appeal, revision) available. But discretion.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Government argues alternative remedy exists.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show alternative remedy is inadequate, not efficacious, or causes delay.
loopholes.courtStrategy: SC: alternative remedy not absolute bar to writ.

title: Right to Property
definition: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
simplifiedExplanation: Right to property is no longer fundamental right (repealed by 44th Amendment 1978). Now constitutional right under Article 300A. Government can acquire property but must follow legal procedure and provide compensation.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons
realWorldExample: Government acquired farmers' land for highway project without adequate compensation. Farmers challenged under Article 300A. Court held compensation must be fair and reasonable.

importantCases.caseName: K.T. Plantation vs State of Karnataka
importantCases.summary: Article 300A right to property is constitutional right. Acquisition must be by law with compensation.

loopholes.description: "Adequate compensation" is undefined. Government determines amount unilaterally.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Government offers minimal compensation.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Land Acquisition Act 2013 provides compensation at market rate + 100% solatium.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge under Article 300A if compensation illusory.

title: No Tax Without Law
definition: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
simplifiedExplanation: Government cannot impose ANY tax without a valid law enacted by Parliament or State Legislature. Every tax must have legislative sanction. This is the foundation of "no taxation without representation".
whoItAppliesTo: Government, all taxpayers
realWorldExample: Municipal corporation levied a new garbage collection fee without any municipal law authorizing it. Citizens challenged under Article 265. Court struck it down.

importantCases.caseName: J.K. Synthetics vs CIT
importantCases.summary: Tax must be imposed by clear statutory language. No implied taxation.

loopholes.description: Government issues circulars/notifications creating de facto taxes without legislation.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Executive orders impose new "fees" or "charges" that are actually taxes.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Fee must have quid pro quo (service in return). If no service, it is tax requiring law.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Test: is it a fee with service or tax without service?

title: Finance Commission
definition: President shall constitute a Finance Commission within 2 years of commencement and thereafter every 5 years. Commission recommends distribution of tax revenues between Centre and States.
simplifiedExplanation: Finance Commission is constituted every 5 years to recommend how tax money is shared between Centre and States. Chairperson + 4 members. Recommendations binding? Mostly followed.
whoItAppliesTo: Centre, States, Finance Commission
realWorldExample: 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) recommended states' share of central taxes at 41%. This determines how much money states get from central tax pool.

importantCases.caseName: Bimal Jalan vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Finance Commission recommendations have force of law when accepted by Presidential Order.

loopholes.description: Finance Commission recommendations are not legally binding. Government can deviate.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Centre does not fully implement FC recommendations.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Political pressure and convention ensure mostly followed. No legal remedy.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Public opinion and state pressure.

title: Election Commission
definition: Superintendence, direction and control of all elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President shall be vested in an Election Commission consisting of Chief Election Commissioner and such Election Commissioners as President may fix.
simplifiedExplanation: Election Commission supervises ALL elections in India. CEC + Election Commissioners. Independent constitutional body. Can issue Model Code of Conduct, conduct elections, register political parties.
whoItAppliesTo: Election Commission, all voters, political parties
realWorldExample: EC announced dates for 2024 Lok Sabha elections. Enforced Model Code of Conduct against parties violating rules. Ordered repoll in booths where irregularities found.

importantCases.caseName: Election Commission vs Saka Venkata Rao
importantCases.summary: EC has power to order repoll, postpone elections, and take all necessary actions for free and fair elections.

loopholes.description: CEC appointed by President on government advice. No independent selection committee.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Government appoints partisan CEC.
loopholes.howToOvercome: 2018 SC directed selection by PM, CJI, LoP committee. Awaiting legislation.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Pending reform.

title: National Emergency
definition: President can proclaim National Emergency if security of India or any part is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
simplifiedExplanation: Emergency on war, aggression, armed rebellion. Post-44th Amendment: requires Cabinet advice, parliamentary approval within 1 month (special majority), judicially reviewable. Declared 3 times: 1962, 1971, 1975.
whoItAppliesTo: Entire India
realWorldExample: 1975 Emergency: PM Indira Gandhi advised Emergency citing "internal disturbance". FRs suspended, press censored, opposition jailed for 21 months. Led to 44th Amendment.

importantCases.caseName: Minerva Mills vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Struck down parts of 42nd Amendment that limited judicial review during Emergency. Basic structure protected.

loopholes.description: President satisfaction means Cabinet advice.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: 1975 Emergency was politically motivated.
loopholes.howToOvercome: 44th Amendment: written Cabinet advice required, "armed rebellion" replaces "internal disturbance", judicial review.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge on mala fides.

title: President Rule (State Emergency)
definition: If President satisfied state cannot be governed constitutionally, may assume state functions, dissolve or suspend state assembly.
simplifiedExplanation: President Rule when state government fails. Misused 100+ times for political purposes. S.R. Bommai (1994) severely restricted misuse — floor test required, judicial review available.
whoItAppliesTo: Individual states
realWorldExample: After 1977 Emergency, Janata Party dismissed 9 Congress state governments. SR Bommai case stopped this pattern.

importantCases.caseName: S.R. Bommai vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: President satisfaction based on relevant material required. Floor test before dismissal. Judicial review available.

loopholes.description: Governor (central appointee) sends biased report against opposition government.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Governors create pretext for President Rule.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Post-Bommai: Governor report not conclusive. Floor test mandatory.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge factual basis and demand floor test.

title: Power to Amend the Constitution
definition: Parliament may amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision following the procedure laid down.
simplifiedExplanation: Parliament can amend Constitution by special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present/voting). Some amendments need ratification by half the states. Basic structure cannot be altered.
whoItAppliesTo: Parliament
realWorldExample: 101st Amendment (GST) required both special majority in Parliament and ratification by more than half states as it affected Centre-State tax distribution.

importantCases.caseName: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala
importantCases.summary: 13-judge bench: Parliament cannot alter basic structure of Constitution. Basic structure includes supremacy of Constitution, republic, secularism, federalism, separation of powers.

loopholes.description: No exhaustive list of basic structure features. Judge-made.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Parliament pushes boundaries arguing feature not part of basic structure.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Several features consistently recognized: judicial review, federalism, secularism, separation of powers.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Argue from accumulated precedent.

title: Special Status for Jammu and Kashmir (Abrogated)
definition: Temporary provisions with respect to Jammu and Kashmir. Limited Parliament's power to make laws for J&K. Abrogated on August 5, 2019 by Presidential Order CO 272 and Parliament resolution.
simplifiedExplanation: Article 370 gave special autonomous status to J&K: separate constitution, dual citizenship, restricted property rights for outsiders. Abrogated in 2019, J&K reorganized into two Union Territories.
whoItAppliesTo: Jammu and Kashmir
realWorldExample: On August 5, 2019, Home Minister Amit Shah announced abrogation of Article 370 in Rajya Sabha. J&K placed under direct central rule. Extensive security measures imposed.

importantCases.caseName: Sampat Prakash vs State of J&K
importantCases.summary: Article 370 has become permanent feature. Cannot be abrogated except with J&K Constituent Assembly consent.

loopholes.description: Whether abrogation via Governor (acting on President order) was valid when state was under President Rule is debated.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Challenged in SC that abrogation requires J&K Constituent Assembly consent.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Multiple petitions pending in SC. Final decision awaited.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Constitutional challenge ongoing.

title: FIR — Information in Cognizable Cases (Zero FIR)
definition: Every information relating to cognizable offence given orally shall be reduced to writing, read to informant, signed, and entered in prescribed book. Copy given free of cost. Can be filed at any police station (Zero FIR).
simplifiedExplanation: Police MUST register FIR for cognizable offences. Zero FIR allows filing at ANY police station, not just jurisdictional one. FIR can be filed electronically. If police refuse, complain to SP or Magistrate under Section 175 BNSS.
punishment: Police refusal leads to departmental action. Police Act Section 170 for dereliction.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person reporting cognizable offence
realWorldExample: Rekha robbed at bus stop in South Delhi. Nearest police station refused saying crime happened elsewhere. She insisted on Zero FIR — police legally obligated to register and transfer.

importantCases.caseName: Lalita Kumari vs Govt of UP
importantCases.summary: FIR registration is MANDATORY for cognizable offences. Police have NO discretion to refuse. Preliminary inquiry only in exceptional cases.

loopholes.description: Despite mandate, police still refuse FIRs, especially against influential persons.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Police tell complainants to settle matter, come later, or register Daily Diary.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Approach Magistrate under Section 175 BNSS. Complain to SP/Commissioner. Online complaint.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show evidence of approaching police station and their refusal.

writ.writDescription: If police refuse FIR, Mandamus can be filed in HC directing police to register FIR.
writ.writExample: Victim approaches HC when local police refuse to file FIR.

title: Bail Provisions — Undertrial Release
definition: Person accused of non-bailable offence may be released on bail. If undertrial has served HALF the maximum imprisonment period, bail must be granted (except for death penalty offences).
simplifiedExplanation: Bail is rule, jail is exception. BNSS introduces safeguard: if undertrial served half maximum sentence, mandatory bail (except death penalty cases). Reduces undertrial population.
whoItAppliesTo: Any accused person in custody
realWorldExample: Ramesh arrested for minor theft (max 3 years). Couldn't afford lawyer, remained in jail 2 years. Under Section 479, since he served more than half maximum sentence, court obligated to release.

importantCases.caseName: Satender Kumar Antil vs CBI
importantCases.summary: Bail is rule, jail exception. Directed use of Section 479 (then 436A CrPC) to release undertrials served half sentence.

loopholes.description: Mandatory bail does not apply to death-eligible offences.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Prosecution argues death-eligible charges even if unlikely to prevent bail.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Argue bail on merits. If prosecution case weak, bail granted regardless of penalty.
loopholes.courtStrategy: File bail citing delay, weak case, bail is rule principle.

title: Arrest Procedure and Safeguards
definition: Arrest requires actual touching/confining body unless submitted. No woman arrest after sunset/sunrise except exceptional circumstances. Woman arrested by woman officer. Must inform grounds immediately.
simplifiedExplanation: Rights when arrested: (1) told why arrested, (2) no woman arrest at night, (3) inform person of choice, (4) magistrate within 24 hrs, (5) consult lawyer, (6) handcuffs only if habitual offender. Arrest memo mandatory.
punishment: Police violating arrest procedures face disciplinary action and contempt.
whoItAppliesTo: Police making arrests, persons being arrested
realWorldExample: Deepak arrested from office by plainclothes officers without warrant. Family didn't know for 36 hrs. Lawyer filed habeas corpus. Court reprimanded police for violating D.K. Basu guidelines.

importantCases.caseName: D.K. Basu vs State of WB
importantCases.summary: 11 mandatory arrest requirements: memo, family info, medical exam, lawyer, no torture, no handcuff, magistrate within 24 hrs.

loopholes.description: Despite D.K. Basu, custodial torture remains common. CCTV not universal.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Police use informal detention ("just for questioning") to avoid formal arrest.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Insist on arrest memo and immediate lawyer access. If tortured, file NHRC complaint.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Document injuries, file habeas corpus.

writ.writDescription: If illegally arrested, HC can be filed to produce detained person.
writ.writExample: Family files HC when person not produced before magistrate within 24 hrs.

title: Electronic Records as Evidence
definition: Any information in electronic record printed on paper, stored in optical/magnetic media or semiconductor memory produced by computer or communication device shall be admissible as document without further proof of original.
simplifiedExplanation: Digital evidence — emails, WhatsApp, CCTV, GPS, call records — admissible. Certificate under Section 39(2) needed. Simplified procedure for electronic evidence admission.
whoItAppliesTo: All parties in legal proceedings
realWorldExample: In dowry case, wife produced WhatsApp messages demanding Rs 10 lakhs. Court admitted after verifying through phone IMEI records, WhatsApp server data, and forensic lab certificate.

importantCases.caseName: Anvar P.V. vs P.K. Basheer
importantCases.summary: Electronic evidence MUST be certified under Section 65B (now Section 39 BSA) to be admissible. Oral evidence insufficient.

importantCases.caseName: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar vs Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
importantCases.summary: Certificate must be furnished when electronic evidence produced. Court can condone delay.

loopholes.description: Electronic evidence easily tampered. Screenshots manipulated, metadata altered.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Parties produce fabricated screenshots, edited recordings.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Insist on forensic examination, hash value verification, server-side records.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge evidence by demanding original device and service provider records.

title: Confession to Police Not Admissible
definition: No confession made to police officer shall be proved against accused. No confession while in police custody unless made in immediate presence of Magistrate.
simplifiedExplanation: Confession to police CANNOT be used in court. Protects against police torture. Confession must be before Magistrate. Exception: fact discovered from confession (Section 27) is admissible.
whoItAppliesTo: All accused persons in criminal cases
realWorldExample: Karim "confessed" after 48 hours without sleep. Court excluded confession under Section 23 — made to police, not magistrate.

importantCases.caseName: Nandini Satpathy vs P.L. Dani
importantCases.summary: Right against self-incrimination extends to police interrogation. Right to remain silent.

loopholes.description: If accused statement leads to discovery of fact (e.g., "I buried knife under tree"), that portion admissible.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Police fabricate discoveries — plant evidence and claim accused led to it.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Independent witnesses (panchas) during recovery, videography, proper forensic handling.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Challenge discovery by showing police already knew independently.

title: Courts to Try All Civil Suits
definition: Courts shall have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred.
simplifiedExplanation: Civil courts have jurisdiction over ALL civil disputes unless specific law bars it. This is the foundational provision for civil litigation. If jurisdiction is barred, bar must be explicit.
whoItAppliesTo: All civil courts, parties to civil disputes
realWorldExample: Property dispute between two families. One party argued civil court cannot hear because it involves caste issue. Court held civil suits maintainable unless expressly barred.

importantCases.caseName: Dhulabhai vs State of MP
importantCases.summary: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction must be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. Civil courts jurisdiction is plenary.

loopholes.description: Determining if jurisdiction is "impliedly barred" is subjective.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defendants argue implied bar to avoid civil suit.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Ouster must be clear and unambiguous. If in doubt, civil court has jurisdiction.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply Dhulabhai test: exclusion must be explicitly or clearly implied.

title: Who May Be Joined as Plaintiffs
definition: All persons may be joined in one suit as plaintiffs where: (a) any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction; and (b) if such persons brought separate suits, any common question of law or fact would arise.
simplifiedExplanation: Multiple persons can file a single suit if their claims arise from the same transaction and common questions would arise. Prevents multiplicity of litigation.
whoItAppliesTo: All civil litigants
realWorldExample: 50 flat buyers in same building defect case can join as co-plaintiffs in single suit against builder.

importantCases.caseName: Bollya vs State of Karnataka
importantCases.summary: Liberal approach to joinder of parties. If common question arises, joinder should be permitted.

loopholes.description: Joining too many parties with different claims can complicate trial.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Plaintiffs join unrelated parties to increase pressure on defendant.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Court can order separate trials or strike out parties not necessary for adjudication.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply for separation of trials.

title: Temporary Injunctions
definition: Court may grant temporary injunction to restrain a party from doing a particular act or to compel performance of an act until disposal of suit. Conditions: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury.
simplifiedExplanation: Temporary injunction is emergency relief to prevent harm during pendency of suit. Three conditions: (1) prima facie case, (2) balance of convenience in favor of applicant, (3) irreparable injury if injunction not granted.
punishment: Violation of injunction = civil contempt, arrest, detention, attachment of property.
whoItAppliesTo: Parties in civil suits seeking interim protection
realWorldExample: Builder started construction blocking neighbour's light and air. Neighbour filed suit and sought temporary injunction. Court granted injunction stopping construction until final hearing.

importantCases.caseName: Wander Ltd vs Antox India P Ltd
importantCases.summary: Balance of convenience must favor injunction. Court should not grant injunction if damages are adequate remedy.

loopholes.description: Courts grant ex-parte injunctions without hearing other side. Used to harass opponents.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Parties obtain ex-parte injunctions on false prima facie case to pressure opponents.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Ex-parte injunction valid for limited period. Must hear other side before extending.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Vacate by showing no prima facie case or balance of convenience.

scenarioTags: need urgent court order to stop harm

title: Mandamus — We Command
definition: A writ issued by court commanding a public authority to perform a public duty imposed by law. Available when authority fails to act and there is no other adequate remedy.
simplifiedExplanation: "We command" — court orders a government official to do their legal duty. Conditions: (1) legal right of applicant, (2) corresponding legal duty of authority, (3) duty of public nature, (4) applicant demanded performance and was refused.
whoItAppliesTo: Public authorities, government officials, tribunals, courts
realWorldExample: Municipal corporation fails to clear garbage for months. Resident filed Mandamus in HC directing them to perform statutory duty of waste collection. HC ordered removal and regular collection schedule.

importantCases.caseName: Bar Council of UP vs State of UP
importantCases.summary: Mandamus lies against public authority for failure to perform mandatory duty. No mandamus against private individuals.

loopholes.description: Courts usually require exhaustion of alternative remedies before granting mandamus.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Authority argues applicant has alternative remedy (appeal, complaint).
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show alternative remedy is inadequate, too slow, or not efficacious.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Mandamus is discretionary. Court may still refuse if alternative exists.

title: Certiorari — Quash the Order
definition: A writ issued to quash the order of a lower court, tribunal, or quasi-judicial authority when it has acted without jurisdiction, exceeded jurisdiction, or violated natural justice.
simplifiedExplanation: "To be certified" — higher court quashes illegal orders of lower courts/tribunals. Grounds: (1) want of jurisdiction, (2) excess of jurisdiction, (3) violation of natural justice, (4) error of law apparent on record, (5) perverse findings.
whoItAppliesTo: Lower courts, tribunals, administrative authorities
realWorldExample: Labour Tribunal passed order against factory without hearing their side (violation of natural justice). Factory filed Certiorari in HC. HC quashed the order and remanded for fresh hearing.

importantCases.caseName: S.L. Kapoor vs Jagmohan
importantCases.summary: Certiorari granted when there is error of law apparent on face of record. Not every error — only manifest error.

loopholes.description: Not every error qualifies — must be error "apparent on face of record" without lengthy argument.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Authority argues error requires detailed examination — not apparent, so certiorari not available.
loopholes.howToOvercome: If error requires lengthy argument, it is not apparent. Focus on clear jurisdictional errors.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show error is manifest without requiring evidence.

title: Prohibition — Stop the Proceedings
definition: A writ issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal prohibiting it from proceeding with a case that is beyond its jurisdiction. Preventive remedy, not corrective.
simplifiedExplanation: "To prohibit" — higher court stops lower court from hearing a case it has no jurisdiction over. Preventive (issued BEFORE order is passed). Different from certiorari which is corrective (after order).
whoItAppliesTo: Lower courts, tribunals acting without/exceeding jurisdiction
realWorldExample: Civil judge started hearing a case exclusively triable by High Court. Party filed Prohibition in HC. HC prohibited civil judge from continuing — case transferred to correct court.

importantCases.caseName: Anisminic vs Foreign Compensation Commission
importantCases.summary: Prohibition lies when tribunal exceeds jurisdiction or acts in excess of its authority.

loopholes.description: Prohibition available only BEFORE order. If order already passed, certiorari is remedy.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Parties confuse prohibition with certiorari and apply too late after order passed.
loopholes.howToOvercome: If order already passed, seek certiorari to quash, not prohibition.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Distinguish: prohibition prevents, certiorari corrects.

title: Quo Warranto — By What Authority
definition: A writ issued to challenge the legal right of a person to hold a public office. Court inquires "by what authority" does the person hold the office.
simplifiedExplanation: "By what warrant" — challenges a person's right to hold public office. Conditions: (1) office is public and substantive, (2) created by Constitution/statute, (3) person occupying office without legal qualification, (4) applicant need not have personal interest — any citizen can file.
whoItAppliesTo: Persons holding public office without authority
realWorldExample: A person was appointed as Chairman of a state commission who did not meet the statutory qualification of "judicial officer". A citizen filed Quo Warranto. HC declared appointment void and ousted the person from office.

importantCases.caseName: University of Mysore vs Govinda Rao
importantCases.summary: Quo Warranto lies only against public offices of substantive character. Not against private offices.

loopholes.description: Quo Warranto is discretionary. Court may refuse if not in public interest.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Persons occupying office argue ouster would disrupt administration.
loopholes.howToOvercome: If person clearly unqualified, court should exercise discretion in favor of ouster.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Public interest in removing unqualified person outweighs disruption.

title: What Agreements Are Contracts
definition: All agreements are contracts if made by free consent of parties competent to contract, for lawful consideration and lawful object, and not expressly declared void.
simplifiedExplanation: Valid contract needs: (1) free consent, (2) competent parties (18+, sound mind), (3) lawful consideration, (4) lawful object, (5) not void by law.
punishment: Not applicable — civil remedy (damages, specific performance).
whoItAppliesTo: Parties entering into agreements
realWorldExample: Ravi agreed to sell car to Sneha. Both adults, lawful consideration, selling car is lawful. Valid contract under Section 10.

importantCases.caseName: Balfour vs Balfour
importantCases.summary: Domestic arrangements not intended to create legal relations — not contracts.

loopholes.description: Difficult to prove consent was not free — undue influence where one party dominates.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Dominant party gets unfair contracts signed by exploiting position.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Burden shifts to dominant party to prove no undue influence (Section 16).
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show dominance, unfairness, no real choice.

title: Compensation for Breach of Contract
definition: Party suffering from breach entitled to compensation as naturally arose from breach, or which parties knew at contract time would likely result from breach.
simplifiedExplanation: Claim compensation for losses that naturally/directly resulted from breach. Cannot claim remote damages. Must mitigate losses — cannot let them pile up.
whoItAppliesTo: Party who suffered loss due to breach
realWorldExample: Wedding venue cancelled 3 days before. Family can claim: difference in cost of new venue, extra decoration, guest transportation. Cannot claim: emotional distress (too remote).

importantCases.caseName: Hadley vs Baxendale
importantCases.summary: Damages must be naturally arising from breach or within contemplation of parties at contract time.
importantCases.significance: Foundational case for contract damages worldwide.

loopholes.description: Difficult to prove exact monetary value of consequential losses.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Breaching party argues losses are speculative or remote.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Maintain detailed records of expenses, alternatives, communications.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Provide documentary evidence: invoices, receipts, market rate comparisons.

title: Grounds for Divorce
definition: Marriage may be dissolved on grounds: (i) adultery; (ii) cruelty; (iii) desertion 2+ years; (iv) conversion; (v) unsound mind; (vi) leprosy; (vii) missing 7+ years. Wife: additional grounds including husband alive from pre-Act marriage, rape/bestiality, maintenance order non-compliance.
simplifiedExplanation: Hindu divorce on fault grounds: cruelty, adultery, desertion, etc. Mutual consent under Section 13B if both agree. Cruelty includes mental cruelty.
whoItAppliesTo: Hindu married couples (also Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs)
realWorldExample: Anita endured years of mental cruelty — humiliation, false accusations, denied work. Divorce granted under Section 13(1)(ia) cruelty.

importantCases.caseName: V. Bhagat vs D. Bhagat
importantCases.summary: Mental cruelty broadly defined: filing false cases, false allegations, persistent nagging.

importantCases.caseName: Naveen Kohli vs Neelu Kohli
importantCases.summary: Recommended "irretrievable breakdown" as divorce ground.

loopholes.description: Mental cruelty is subjective. What is cruel to one may be acceptable to another.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Both spouses allege mental cruelty — normal disagreements portrayed as cruelty.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Court examines cumulative effect over time, social/economic background.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Document instances with dates, specifics. Medical records of depression/anxiety.

title: Conditions for Special Marriage
definition: Marriage under SMA requires: (a) neither party has spouse living; (b) neither is idiot/lunatic; (c) male 21+, female 18+; (d) not within prohibited relationship; (e) if custom permits marriage between prohibited degrees, allowed.
simplifiedExplanation: SMA allows inter-faith and inter-caste civil marriage without religious ceremony. Conditions apply: age, no existing spouse, sound mind, not prohibited relationship. Notice to Marriage Officer required for 30 days.
whoItAppliesTo: Any two persons in India regardless of religion
realWorldExample: Hindu girl and Muslim boy want to marry without conversion. They register under SMA. After 30-day notice with no valid objections, Marriage Officer solemnizes marriage.

importantCases.caseName: Lata Singh vs State of UP
importantCases.summary: Major inter-caste/inter-faith couples have right to marry under SMA. Police must protect them from family harassment.
importantCases.significance: Right to marry person of choice.

loopholes.description: 30-day notice period allows relatives/community members to file frivolous objections.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Families file baseless objections to prevent marriage.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Marriage Officer decides objections. If frivolous, reject and proceed.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Approach HC for protection if objections are harassing.

lawName: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
title: Application to Magistrate for Protection Orders
definition: Aggrieved person or any person on her behalf may apply to Magistrate for one or more reliefs under this Act. Magistrate shall within 3 days fix first date of hearing.
simplifiedExplanation: Woman can directly approach Magistrate for protection from domestic violence. Can get: (1) protection order (stop violence), (2) residence order (stay in shared household), (3) monetary relief (maintenance), (4) custody orders, (5) compensation. Emergency relief within days.
punishment: Violation of protection order: up to 1 year and/or fine up to Rs 20,000.
whoItAppliesTo: Women in domestic relationships (includes wife, mother, sister, live-in partner)
realWorldExample: Sunita's husband beats her and throws her out of house. She files application under Section 12. Magistrate grants: (1) protection order restraining husband, (2) right to stay in house, (3) monthly maintenance of Rs 10,000.

importantCases.caseName: V.D. Bhanot vs Savita Bhandari
importantCases.summary: DV Act covers women in live-in relationships, not just married women.

loopholes.description: DV Act provisions are used by wives to file false complaints during matrimonial disputes.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Wives file DV cases as counter-weapon in custody/property disputes.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Courts carefully examine relationship, violence allegations, timeline.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Apply for quashing if allegations are patently false.

title: Definition of Consumer
definition: "Consumer" means any person who buys goods or hires services for consideration paid/promised, but does not include person who buys for resale or commercial purpose.
simplifiedExplanation: Consumer is someone who buys goods/services for personal use, not for resale. Includes online purchases. Covers both goods and services (including telecom, banking, insurance, healthcare).
whoItAppliesTo: Any person buying goods or using services for personal use
realWorldExample: Priya bought a defective laptop from Amazon for personal use. She is a consumer. She bought 50 laptops to resell — not a consumer.

importantCases.caseName: Lucknow Development Authority vs M.K. Gupta
importantCases.summary: Housing authorities provide "service" — flat buyers are consumers. Services include government/public authorities.

loopholes.description: Person buying for commercial purpose NOT a consumer. "Commercial purpose" broadly interpreted.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Sellers argue buyer uses product commercially even when primarily for personal use.
loopholes.howToOvercome: If goods used mainly for earning livelihood (auto driver buying vehicle), still consumer.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show primary purpose is self-employment, not large-scale commercial.

title: Computer Related Offences
definition: If any person dishonestly or fraudulently does any act referred to in Section 43 (unauthorized access, downloading, introduction of virus, disruption, denial of service), he shall be punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh or both.
simplifiedExplanation: Covers unauthorized access to computer systems, data theft, virus introduction, denial of service attacks. Requires dishonest/fraudulent intention. Broad scope covering most hacking activities.
punishment: Up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs 5 lakh.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who unauthorizedly accesses computers
realWorldExample: Employee of a company copied client database before quitting and shared it with competitor. Charged under Section 66 for dishonest computer access and data theft.

importantCases.caseName: Poona Auto Ancillaries vs P.S. Dhole
importantCases.summary: Employer not liable for employee's criminal act under Section 66 when employee acted beyond scope of employment.

loopholes.description: Prosecution must prove dishonest or fraudulent intention. Accused says it was authorized or accidental.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Accused claims they had authorization or didn't know access was unauthorized.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show lack of authorization through system logs, access controls, termination of employment.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Access logs and IP tracking establish unauthorized access.

title: Right to Information
definition: All citizens shall have the right to information, subject to provisions of this Act.
simplifiedExplanation: Every citizen can request information from any public authority. Authority must reply within 30 days (48 hrs for life/liberty). Information includes records, documents, emails, opinions, samples. Exemptions include national security, personal information, cabinet papers, commercial confidence.
punishment: Penalty of Rs 250 per day for delay beyond 30 days (max Rs 25,000).
whoItAppliesTo: All citizens of India
realWorldExample: Citizen filed RTI asking how many toilets built under Swachh Bharat in her village. Block Development Officer refused. She appealed to Information Commission. Commission directed disclosure within 15 days.

importantCases.caseName: CBSE vs Aditya Bandopadhyay
importantCases.summary: RTI applies to examination bodies. Answer sheets can be disclosed. Citizens can access evaluation process.

loopholes.description: Public authorities cite exemptions broadly to deny information. "Commercial confidence" and "personal information" used to hide corruption.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Officials deny information claiming exemption even when public interest outweighs.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Public interest test — if disclosure serves public interest, exemption cannot be claimed.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Appeal to Information Commission. Prove public interest in disclosure.

title: Penetrative Sexual Assault
definition: A person commits penetrative sexual assault if he penetrates his penis or any object into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a child, or makes the child do so with him or another person.
simplifiedExplanation: Sexual assault on a child (under 18). Includes penile, digital, and object penetration. No consent defense. Both male and female victims covered. Gender neutral.
punishment: Minimum 10 years to life imprisonment and fine. Aggravated: 20 years to death.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who commits sexual assault on a child
realWorldExample: School teacher molested a 7-year-old student repeatedly. Charged under POCSO Section 3 (penetrative sexual assault). Sentenced to 20 years.

importantCases.caseName: Independent Thought vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Sexual intercourse with wife below 18 is rape under POCSO, reading down IPC marital rape exception for minors.
importantCases.significance: Protects child brides from marital rape.

loopholes.description: POCSO cases often filed in matrimonial/property disputes involving children.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: One parent accuses other of POCSO to gain custody advantage.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Courts examine evidence carefully — delay, motive, child's statement consistency.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Forensic evidence, medical reports, child psychology evaluation.

title: Motor Accident Claims
definition: Application for compensation arising out of motor accident may be made to Claims Tribunal by person who sustained injury, owner of property, or legal representative of deceased.
simplifiedExplanation: Victims of road accidents or their families can claim compensation from Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT). No fault liability: even if victim negligent, minimum compensation payable. Third party insurance mandatory.
whoItAppliesTo: Road accident victims, their families
realWorldExample: Rajat died in bus-truck collision. His wife filed claim under Section 166. Tribunal awarded Rs 25 lakh compensation from insurance company under third party policy.

importantCases.caseName: R.S. Sood vs High Court of Rajasthan
importantCases.summary: Third party claims under Section 166 are quasi-judicial. Tribunal must determine just compensation considering all factors.

loopholes.description: Gangs stage fake accidents to claim insurance money.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Fraudsters fabricate accident claims with fake medical reports.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Insurance companies investigate thoroughly. Courts examine circumstances, medical evidence, police reports.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Cross-examination of claimants, independent investigation.

title: Cleanliness in Factories
definition: Every factory shall be kept clean and free from effluent flowing from drains and sanitary conveniences. Precautions against dust, fumes, and other impurities.
simplifiedExplanation: Factories must maintain cleanliness: clean floors, proper drainage, ventilation, waste disposal. Worker health and hygiene protected.
punishment: Up to Rs 2 lakh fine and/or imprisonment up to 2 years for violations.
whoItAppliesTo: All factory owners and occupiers
realWorldExample: Factory workers developed respiratory problems due to dust without exhaust system. Labour inspector found violation of Section 11. Owner fined Rs 50,000.

importantCases.caseName: Ratanlal vs State of MP
importantCases.summary: Factory owner cannot escape liability by delegating cleanliness to manager.

scenarioTags: workers fall sick due to factory conditions

title: Prohibition on Handling Hazardous Substances
definition: No person shall handle or cause to be handled any hazardous substance except in accordance with prescribed procedures and after complying with safety standards.
simplifiedExplanation: Businesses handling hazardous substances must follow strict safety procedures, obtain authorization, disclose emergency plans. Covers chemical factories, battery manufacturers, paint industries.
punishment: Up to 5 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs 1 lakh. Continuing offence: additional Rs 5,000 per day.
whoItAppliesTo: Industries and persons handling hazardous substances
realWorldExample: Chemical factory stored toxic waste illegally near residential area. Leakage caused hospitalization of 50 residents. Factory owner charged under Section 7 EPA for unauthorized handling of hazardous substance.

importantCases.caseName: M.C. Mehta vs Union of India (Ganga Pollution)
importantCases.summary: Absolute liability for hazardous industries handling toxic substances. Cannot escape liability by claiming all precautions taken.

loopholes.description: Companies outsource hazardous waste handling to unlicensed third parties to evade liability.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Company claims waste disposal done by licensed contractor.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Principal company remains liable for waste generated by its process.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Prove waste was generated from company's process.

title: Rape
definition: A man commits rape if he penetrates, inserts any object or body part into the vagina, urethra, anus of a woman, or applies his mouth to those areas, under circumstances including against her will, without consent, consent obtained by fear/fraud, or when she cannot communicate consent. Replaces IPC Section 375.
simplifiedExplanation: Rape defined broadly to include any non-consensual sexual act. Age of consent 18. Marital rape exception: sex with wife above 18 is not rape.
punishment: Minimum 10 years RI, extendable to life. Gang rape min 20 years to life. Minor under 12: min 20 years to death.
whoItAppliesTo: A man can be charged; victim must be a woman.
realWorldExample: Meera drugged at party and assaulted while unconscious. Court held consent under intoxication invalid. Accused convicted under Section 63.

importantCases.caseName: Mukesh vs State of NCT Delhi (Nirbhaya)
importantCases.summary: Upheld death for gang-rape and murder. Led to Criminal Law Amendment 2013.

importantCases.caseName: Independent Thought vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Read down marital rape exception for wives aged 15-18.

loopholes.description: Sex with own wife above 18 is not rape under Exception 2.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Husbands cannot be prosecuted for raping wives.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Challenge under Article 14, 21. Petition pending in SC.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Argue colonial relic inconsistent with constitutional values.

loopholes.description: No specific punishment for false rape accusations.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: False allegations used as leverage in matrimonial disputes.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Examine FIR timeline, relationship context, corroborative evidence.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Look at medical reports, electronic evidence, witness statements.

title: Punishment for Rape
definition: Whoever commits rape under Section 63 shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for not less than 10 years, extendable to life, and fine.
simplifiedExplanation: Minimum 10 years for rape. Gang rape: minimum 20 years to life. Minor under 16: min 20 years. Minor under 12: 20 to death.
punishment: Minimum 10 years RI to life. Aggravated: 20 years to death.
whoItAppliesTo: Person convicted of rape
realWorldExample: Man convicted of raping 10-year-old sentenced to 25 years RI.

title: Murder
definition: Except in excepted cases, culpable homicide is murder if: (1) done with intention of causing death; (2) done with intention of causing injury known to be likely to cause death; (3) intended injury sufficient in ordinary course to cause death; (4) act so imminently dangerous that death is probable. Replaces IPC Section 300.
simplifiedExplanation: Murder requires intention to kill or cause injuries sufficient to cause death. Distinguished from culpable homicide not amounting to murder by presence of intention.
punishment: Death or life imprisonment and fine. Death penalty reserved for rarest of rare cases.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who commits murder.
realWorldExample: Vikram, in property dispute, stabbed neighbor multiple times in chest causing death. Charged under Section 101 BNS.

importantCases.caseName: Bachan Singh vs State of Punjab
importantCases.summary: Death penalty constitutional but only in rarest of rare cases.

importantCases.caseName: K.M. Nanavati vs State of Maharashtra
importantCases.summary: Last jury trial in India. Distinguished murder from culpable homicide.
importantCases.significance: Led to abolition of jury trials.

importantCases.caseName: Machhi Singh vs State of Punjab
importantCases.summary: Categories where death penalty may be warranted.

loopholes.description: If killing falls under exceptions (provocation, self-defence exceeded, sudden fight), it becomes culpable homicide, not murder.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues grave and sudden provocation to reduce charge.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Prove provocation was NOT sudden. Show premeditation.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Establish premeditation through evidence of weapon, prior threats.

loopholes.description: Without eyewitnesses, chain must be complete pointing only to accused.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues chain is incomplete.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Build complete chain: motive, opportunity, forensics, post-crime conduct.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Use DNA, CCTV, call records to complete chain.

scenarioTags: difference between murder and culpable homicide

title: Punishment for Murder in Certain Cases (Mob Lynching)
definition: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or life imprisonment if committed by: (a) a previous murder convict; or (b) a group of 5+ on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, language, personal belief — mob lynching provision. New in BNS 2023.
simplifiedExplanation: New provision addressing mob lynching. If 5+ persons commit murder based on caste/religion/community, each faces death or life imprisonment. Fills gap in old IPC after several lynching incidents across India.
punishment: Death or life imprisonment. Mob lynching: death or life (min 7 years) and fine.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person committing murder, especially in mob lynching situations.
realWorldExample: Eight men attacked Muslim cattle trader on suspicion of cow smuggling, beat him with iron rods until death. Each charged under Section 103 BNS.

importantCases.caseName: Tehseen S. Poonawalla vs Union of India
importantCases.summary: Condemned mob lynching. Issued comprehensive guidelines: nodal officers, prompt FIRs, action against failing police.
importantCases.significance: Led to BNS 2023 mob lynching provisions.

loopholes.description: Difficult to prove all 5+ shared common intent to kill based on prohibited ground.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Mob members claim bystanders or personal enmity, not caste/religion motive.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Use Section 3(5) BNS common intention. Gather social media evidence.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Prove common intention through WhatsApp groups, social media posts showing communal motive.

scenarioTags: mob attacked person based on religion

title: Attempt to Commit Offences
definition: Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment and does any act towards its commission shall be punished. Replaces IPC Section 511.
simplifiedExplanation: Attempt is a substantial step toward committing a crime that fails. For murder attempt, up to life imprisonment. Key distinction from preparation (not punishable) is crucial.
punishment: Death attempt: up to 10 years. Life imprisonment attempt: up to 5 years. Other attempts: half maximum sentence.
whoItAppliesTo: Anyone who attempts to commit an offence.
realWorldExample: Rajesh bought gun, went to enemy house, aimed and fired but missed. Guilty of attempt to murder even though murder not completed.

importantCases.caseName: State of Maharashtra vs Mohd. Yakub
importantCases.summary: Distinguished preparation from attempt. For attempt, accused must cross line from preparation to execution.

loopholes.description: Line between preparation and attempt is blurry. Mere preparation is not punishable.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues acts were mere preparation that could have been abandoned.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show accused crossed threshold — done all acts necessary for final offence.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Examine whether accused took last step before actual commission.

title: Grievous Hurt
definition: Whoever causes hurt and the hurt is: emasculation, permanent loss of sight/hearing/limb/joint, fracture/dislocation, or hurt endangering life or causing severe pain for 20+ days or inability to pursue ordinary activities for 20+ days. Replaces IPC Section 320.
simplifiedExplanation: Grievous hurt includes 8 specific types: castration, loss of sight/hearing/limb, fracture, permanent disfigurement, hurt endangering life.
punishment: Up to 7 years and fine. If by dangerous weapon: up to 10 years.
whoItAppliesTo: Anyone who causes grievous hurt.
realWorldExample: Sanjay hit Rohan with iron rod fracturing arm in two places. Fracture qualified as grievous hurt under Section 115.

importantCases.caseName: Jai Prakash vs State of Delhi
importantCases.summary: Fracture not necessary for grievous hurt — hurt endangering life qualifies.

loopholes.description: Classification depends on medical evidence. Initial simple injury may become grievous.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues injury was simple based on initial report.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Get follow-up examinations documenting duration of recovery and complications.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Present extended treatment records and specialist opinions.

title: Kidnapping
definition: (1) Kidnapping from India — taking a person out of India without consent. (2) Kidnapping from lawful guardianship — taking a minor under 16 (male) or 18 (female) from guardian without consent. Replaces IPC Sections 359-361.
simplifiedExplanation: Kidnapping involves taking a person without consent. Two types: taking out of India, or taking a minor from guardian. Abduction is different (compelling by force).
whoItAppliesTo: Anyone who kidnaps another person.
realWorldExample: Neighbor lured 14-year-old girl from school promising film career. Took her to another city without parents knowledge. Charged with kidnapping from guardianship.

importantCases.caseName: S. Varadarajan vs State of Madras
importantCases.summary: When minor voluntarily leaves guardian, accused may not be guilty if there was no taking.

loopholes.description: If minor above 16 (boy) or 18 (girl) goes willingly, kidnapping charge fails.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Accused argues minor came voluntarily and was not taken.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Prove the accused actively induced or enticed the minor to leave.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show accused made promises, gave gifts, or used influence to persuade.

scenarioTags: someone forced to go with another

title: Theft
definition: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of possession of any person without consent, moves that property in order to such taking, commits theft. Replaces IPC Section 378.
simplifiedExplanation: Theft is dishonest taking of movable property without consent. Key elements: dishonest intention, property in possession, taking without consent, moving the property.
punishment: Up to 3 years or fine or both. If committed at night: up to 7 years.
whoItAppliesTo: Anyone who commits theft.
realWorldExample: Rahul took roommates laptop from shared apartment intending to sell it. Charged with theft under Section 303.

importantCases.caseName: R.K. Dalmia vs Delhi Administration
importantCases.summary: Dishonest intention is essence of theft. If accused believed in good faith property was theirs, no theft.

loopholes.description: If accused honestly believed they had right to property, no theft even if wrong.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues accused believed property was theirs.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Prove accused knew property belonged to someone else or claim was unreasonable.
loopholes.courtStrategy: Show accused acted secretly, tried to conceal property.

title: Extortion
definition: Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person or another, and thereby dishonestly induces that person to deliver any property or valuable security, commits extortion. Replaces IPC Section 383.
simplifiedExplanation: Extortion is forcing someone to give property by threatening harm. Key elements: putting in fear and using that fear to obtain property.
punishment: Up to 3 years or fine or both. If aggravated (fear of death/grievous hurt): up to 10 years.
whoItAppliesTo: Anyone who uses threats to obtain property.
realWorldExample: Gang threatened shopkeeper to pay Rs 50,000 monthly protection money or shop would be burnt. Charged with extortion.

importantCases.caseName: R.S. Nayak vs A.R. Antulay
importantCases.summary: Distinguished extortion from bribery. Property obtained by creating fear.

loopholes.description: Must prove threat CAUSED victim to part with property.
loopholes.howPeopleUseIt: Defense argues victim paid voluntarily or for unrelated reasons.
loopholes.howToOvercome: Show timing of payment relative to threat, victim changed behavior.
