definition: Section 59 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 deals with "Penalty for Non-Registration of Projects".
simplifiedExplanation: Selling without RERA registration is a criminal offence. Builder can be jailed for up to 3 years.
punishment: Up to 10% of estimated project cost. Continued violation: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to further 10% or both.
whoItAppliesTo: Real estate promoters, agents, and homebuyers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for non-registration of projects under the RERA.
scenarioTags: penalty for non-registration of projects under RERA

title: Penalty for Non-Registration of Agent
definition: Section 61 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 deals with "Penalty for Non-Registration of Agent".
simplifiedExplanation: Agents who sell without RERA registration face daily penalty. This ensures all agents in the real estate market are registered and accountable.
punishment: ₹10,000/day of default, up to 5% of cost of apartment/plot sold
whoItAppliesTo: Real estate promoters, agents, and homebuyers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for non-registration of agent under the RERA.
scenarioTags: penalty for non-registration of agent under RERA

title: Penalty for Non-Compliance
definition: Section 63 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 deals with "Penalty for Non-Compliance".
simplifiedExplanation: For any contravention of RERA orders or regulations — blanket penalty up to 5% of estimated cost. Continued contravention: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
punishment: Up to 5% of estimated project cost for each violation
whoItAppliesTo: Real estate promoters, agents, and homebuyers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for non-compliance under the RERA.

title: Documents of Which Registration is Compulsory
definition: The following documents shall be registered: (a) instruments of gift of immovable property, (b) leases of immovable property for more than one year, (c) non-testamentary instruments transferring immovable property above ₹100.
simplifiedExplanation: Sale deeds, gift deeds, leases over 1 year, and mortgages (other than equitable) MUST be registered. Without registration, these documents have no legal effect — they cannot be used as evidence of ownership.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to documents of which registration is compulsory under the Registration Act.
tags: documents of which registration is compulsory
aiSearchKeywords: documents of which registration is compulsory
scenarioTags: documents of which registration is compulsory under Registration Act

title: Documents of Which Registration is Optional
definition: Section 18 of the Registration Act 1908 deals with "Documents of Which Registration is Optional".
simplifiedExplanation: Wills, leases under 1 year, movable property documents — registration is optional. But registering a will is recommended for safety.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to documents of which registration is optional under the Registration Act.
tags: documents of which registration is optional
aiSearchKeywords: documents of which registration is optional
scenarioTags: documents of which registration is optional under Registration Act

title: Time for Presenting Documents
definition: Section 23 of the Registration Act 1908 deals with "Time for Presenting Documents".
simplifiedExplanation: Documents must be presented for registration within 4 months of execution. If delayed up to 4 more months, can be registered with late fee and penalty (up to 10x the normal fee).
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to time for presenting documents under the Registration Act.
scenarioTags: time for presenting documents under Registration Act

title: Persons Who Must Present Documents
definition: Section 32 of the Registration Act 1908 deals with "Persons Who Must Present Documents".
simplifiedExplanation: Document must be presented by: (1) the person executing it, (2) their representative or agent with power of attorney, (3) their legal representative (if deceased). Sub-Registrar must verify identity.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to persons who must present documents under the Registration Act.
scenarioTags: persons who must present documents under Registration Act

title: Enquiry Before Registration
definition: Section 34 of the Registration Act 1908 deals with "Enquiry Before Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Sub-Registrar must satisfy himself about the identity of the person appearing before him and that the person is the same who executed the document. This prevents fraudulent registrations.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to enquiry before registration under the Registration Act.
scenarioTags: enquiry before registration under Registration Act

title: Effect of Non-Registration
definition: No document required by Section 17 to be registered shall affect any immovable property or confer any power to adopt, unless it has been registered.
simplifiedExplanation: If a document that MUST be registered is NOT registered, it is legally worthless — it cannot be used to prove ownership, cannot be admitted as evidence (except as evidence of contract under Section 53A TPA), and cannot affect property rights.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons executing or registering documents related to property
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to effect of non-registration under the Registration Act.
scenarioTags: effect of non-registration under Registration Act

title: Benami Transaction Defined
definition: A benami transaction means a transaction where property is held by or transferred to a person (benamidar) for a consideration paid by another person (beneficial owner).
simplifiedExplanation: Benami = property bought in someone else's name using your money. Example: You buy a house in your driver's name to hide your wealth. The driver is the 'benamidar' and you are the 'beneficial owner'. This is illegal.
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment 1-7 years + fine up to 25% of FMV of property
whoItAppliesTo: All persons involved in benami transactions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to benami transaction defined under the Benami Act.
scenarioTags: benami transaction defined under Benami Act

title: Prohibition of Benami Transactions
definition: No person shall enter into any benami transaction. Violation is punishable under this Act.
simplifiedExplanation: ALL benami transactions are prohibited. If caught, the property can be confiscated by the government and both the benamidar and the beneficial owner can be jailed. There are exceptions: property held by Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) member, property held for spouse or children if paid from known sources.
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment 1-7 years + fine up to 25% of fair market value
whoItAppliesTo: All persons involved in benami transactions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of benami transactions under the Benami Act.
scenarioTags: prohibition of benami transactions under Benami Act

title: Property Held Benami — Not Re-Transferable
definition: Section 5 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016 deals with "Property Held Benami — Not Re-Transferable".
simplifiedExplanation: No person claiming to be the real owner of benami property can recover it from the benamidar. And no court can help you get back property held in someone else's name. So if you put property in your driver's name — you lose it.
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment 1-7 years + fine up to 25% of FMV of property
whoItAppliesTo: All persons involved in benami transactions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to property held benami — not re-transferable under the Benami Act.
scenarioTags: property held benami — not re-transferable under Benami Act

title: Confiscation of Benami Property
definition: Section 24 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016 deals with "Confiscation of Benami Property".
simplifiedExplanation: Government can confiscate benami property after an order by the Adjudicating Authority. Property vests in the Central Government. This is permanent — the property is gone forever.
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment 1-7 years + fine up to 25% of FMV of property
whoItAppliesTo: All persons involved in benami transactions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to confiscation of benami property under the Benami Act.
scenarioTags: confiscation of benami property under Benami Act

title: Penalty for Benami Transaction
definition: Section 53 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016 deals with "Penalty for Benami Transaction".
simplifiedExplanation: Both the benamidar (name-lender) and the beneficial owner (real buyer) are punishable. Providing false information about benami property: up to 5 years RI + fine.
punishment: Rigorous imprisonment 1-7 years + fine up to 25% of fair market value of property
whoItAppliesTo: All persons involved in benami transactions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for benami transaction under the Benami Act.
scenarioTags: penalty for benami transaction under Benami Act

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Affected Family Defined
definition: Section 2(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Affected Family Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Affected family includes: (1) family whose land is acquired, (2) family dependent on such land (tenants, share-croppers, artisans, workers), (3) tribals and forest dwellers losing forest rights. All get rehabilitation.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to affected family defined under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: affected family defined under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Public Purpose Defined
definition: Section 3(za) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Public Purpose Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Land can only be acquired for 'public purpose': infrastructure, defence, industrial corridors, housing for poor, planned development. Government CANNOT acquire land for private companies unless public purpose is served.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to public purpose defined under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: public purpose defined under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Preliminary Investigation
definition: Section 10 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Preliminary Investigation".
simplifiedExplanation: Before acquisition, government must do preliminary survey with 30-day notice to landowners. Compensation for damage during survey must be paid. Objections must be heard.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to preliminary investigation under the LARR Act 2013.

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Social Impact Assessment (SIA)
definition: Whenever the Government intends to acquire land, it shall carry out a Social Impact Assessment study in consultation with the concerned Panchayat, Municipality or Municipal Corporation.
simplifiedExplanation: Before acquiring land, government MUST conduct a Social Impact Assessment to evaluate: how many families affected, what alternative sites exist, social impact, minimum displacement principle. This is mandatory.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to social impact assessment (sia) under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: social impact assessment (sia) under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Notification of Preliminary Acquisition
definition: Section 19 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Notification of Preliminary Acquisition".
simplifiedExplanation: After SIA, if government decides to proceed, it publishes preliminary notification in Official Gazette and newspapers. Landowners can file objections within 60 days.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to notification of preliminary acquisition under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: notification of preliminary acquisition under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Determination of Market Value
definition: Section 26 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Determination of Market Value".
simplifiedExplanation: Compensation = higher of: (1) minimum value specified by government, (2) average sale price of similar land in the area over last 3 years, (3) value as per Indian Stamp Act. Multiplied by a factor of 1-2 for rural areas.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to determination of market value under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: determination of market value under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Determination of Amount — Solatium
definition: Section 27 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Determination of Amount — Solatium".
simplifiedExplanation: In ADDITION to market value, affected family gets: 100% solatium (so total = 2x market value in urban areas, 4x in rural areas because of 2x multiplier + 100% solatium on multiplied amount). This replaced the old 30% solatium.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to determination of amount — solatium under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: determination of amount — solatium under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Compensation for Affected Families Other Than Landowners
definition: Section 31 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Compensation for Affected Families Other Than Landowners".
simplifiedExplanation: Families who are NOT landowners but are AFFECTED (labourers, tenants, share-croppers) also get: (1) resettlement allowance, (2) annuity for 20 years, (3) employment in project, (4) one-time financial assistance.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to compensation for affected families other than landowners under the LARR Act 2013.
tags: compensation for affected families other than landowners
aiSearchKeywords: compensation for affected families other than landowners
scenarioTags: compensation for affected families other than landowners under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Consent of Affected Families — Private Projects
definition: Prior consent of at least 80% of affected families shall be obtained for acquisition of land for private projects, and 70% for public-private partnership projects.
simplifiedExplanation: For PRIVATE company projects: 80% landowner consent required. For PPP projects: 70% consent required. For pure government projects: no consent needed. This prevents forced acquisition for private benefit.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to consent of affected families — private projects under the LARR Act 2013.
tags: consent of affected families — private projects
aiSearchKeywords: consent of affected families — private projects
scenarioTags: consent of affected families — private projects under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: Return of Unutilized Land
definition: Section 46 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "Return of Unutilized Land".
simplifiedExplanation: If government acquires land but does NOT use it for 5 years, the land must be returned to the original owner or the State Land Bank. This prevents land-hoarding by government.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to return of unutilized land under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: return of unutilized land under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: National Monitoring Committee
definition: Section 64 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "National Monitoring Committee".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government must constitute a National Monitoring Committee and State Monitoring Committees to review and monitor the R&R (Rehabilitation and Resettlement) implementation.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to national monitoring committee under the LARR Act 2013.
scenarioTags: national monitoring committee under LARR Act 2013

lawName: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013
title: No Change of Purpose Without Consent
definition: Section 101 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 deals with "No Change of Purpose Without Consent".
simplifiedExplanation: Once land is acquired for a stated purpose, the purpose CANNOT be changed without the consent of affected families and payment of additional compensation. Prevents bait-and-switch tactics.
whoItAppliesTo: Government acquiring land and affected landowners/families
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to no change of purpose without consent under the LARR Act 2013.
tags: no change of purpose without consent
aiSearchKeywords: no change of purpose without consent
scenarioTags: no change of purpose without consent under LARR Act 2013

title: Electoral Registration Officer
definition: Section 13D of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Electoral Registration Officer".
simplifiedExplanation: The Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) is responsible for preparing and maintaining the electoral roll of each constituency. They can include or exclude names. Orders can be appealed.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to electoral registration officer under the RPA 1950.

title: Conditions of Registration
definition: Section 14 of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Conditions of Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: A person is entitled to be registered if: (1) Indian citizen, (2) 18+ years old on qualifying date (January 1), (3) ordinarily resident in the constituency. Non-residents, unsound mind persons, and persons disqualified by law cannot register.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to conditions of registration under the RPA 1950.

title: Disqualifications for Registration
definition: Section 16 of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Disqualifications for Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: A person is disqualified from being registered: (1) if not a citizen of India, (2) if of unsound mind declared by court, (3) if disqualified for corrupt or illegal practices under election law.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualifications for registration under the RPA 1950.

title: Electoral Rolls — Manner of Preparation
definition: Section 20 of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Electoral Rolls — Manner of Preparation".
simplifiedExplanation: Electoral rolls are constituency-wise. Rolls are revised annually. Names can be added or removed through applications. Special revision can be ordered before elections.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to electoral rolls — manner of preparation under the RPA 1950.
scenarioTags: electoral rolls — manner of preparation under RPA 1950

title: Right to Vote
definition: Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Right to Vote".
simplifiedExplanation: Every person whose name appears in the electoral roll is entitled to vote in that constituency. No one can vote in more than one constituency. Personating a voter is a criminal offence.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to vote under the RPA 1950.

title: Correction of Entries in Electoral Roll
definition: Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act 1950 deals with "Correction of Entries in Electoral Roll".
simplifiedExplanation: If a name is wrongly included, excluded, or there are errors in details, applications can be filed for correction. ERO must hear and decide. Appeal lies to Chief Electoral Officer.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens aged 18 and above
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to correction of entries in electoral roll under the RPA 1950.
tags: correction of entries in electoral roll
aiSearchKeywords: correction of entries in electoral roll
scenarioTags: correction of entries in electoral roll under RPA 1950

title: Qualifications for Membership of Lok Sabha
definition: Section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Qualifications for Membership of Lok Sabha".
simplifiedExplanation: To be a Lok Sabha member: (1) Indian citizen, (2) 25+ years old, (3) registered as voter in any constituency, (4) not disqualified under any law.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to qualifications for membership of lok sabha under the RPA 1951.
tags: qualifications for membership of lok sabha
aiSearchKeywords: qualifications for membership of lok sabha
scenarioTags: qualifications for membership of lok sabha under RPA 1951

title: Qualifications for Membership of State Legislature
definition: Section 4 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Qualifications for Membership of State Legislature".
simplifiedExplanation: To be MLA/MLC: (1) Indian citizen, (2) 25+ for Assembly, 30+ for Council, (3) registered as voter in any constituency of the state. Same disqualifications apply.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to qualifications for membership of state legislature under the RPA 1951.
tags: qualifications for membership of state legislature
aiSearchKeywords: qualifications for membership of state legislature
scenarioTags: qualifications for membership of state legislature under RPA 1951

title: Qualifications for Membership of Rajya Sabha
definition: Section 5 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Qualifications for Membership of Rajya Sabha".
simplifiedExplanation: To be Rajya Sabha member: (1) Indian citizen, (2) 30+ years old, (3) registered as voter. Rajya Sabha members represent states and are elected by state assembly MLAs.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to qualifications for membership of rajya sabha under the RPA 1951.
tags: qualifications for membership of rajya sabha
aiSearchKeywords: qualifications for membership of rajya sabha
scenarioTags: qualifications for membership of rajya sabha under RPA 1951

title: Disqualification on Conviction
definition: A person convicted of certain offences and sentenced to imprisonment of 2 years or more shall be disqualified from date of conviction for a period extending to 6 years after release.
simplifiedExplanation: If convicted and sentenced to 2+ years in prison — IMMEDIATE disqualification from Parliament/Assembly + cannot contest for 6 years after release. No protection even if appeal is filed (after Lily Thomas 2013).
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualification on conviction under the RPA 1951.

importantCases.caseName: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
importantCases.summary: Struck down Section 8(4) — convicted MPs/MLAs cannot avoid disqualification by merely filing appeal.

title: Disqualification on Conviction for Corrupt Practice
definition: Section 8A of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disqualification on Conviction for Corrupt Practice".
simplifiedExplanation: If a person is convicted of corrupt practice by the court trying an election petition, they are disqualified for 6 years from the date of conviction.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualification on conviction for corrupt practice under the RPA 1951.
tags: disqualification on conviction for corrupt practice
aiSearchKeywords: disqualification on conviction for corrupt practice
scenarioTags: disqualification on conviction for corrupt practice under RPA 1951

title: Disqualification for Dismissal for Corruption
definition: Section 9 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disqualification for Dismissal for Corruption".
simplifiedExplanation: A government servant dismissed for corruption or disloyalty to the State is disqualified for 5 years from date of dismissal.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualification for dismissal for corruption under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: disqualification for dismissal for corruption under RPA 1951

title: Disqualification for Government Contracts
definition: Section 9A of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disqualification for Government Contracts".
simplifiedExplanation: A person who has a subsisting government contract (directly or through a firm) is disqualified from being elected. This prevents conflict of interest.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualification for government contracts under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: disqualification for government contracts under RPA 1951

title: Disqualification for Office Under Government
definition: Section 10 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disqualification for Office Under Government".
simplifiedExplanation: A person holding an office of profit under the Government cannot be a member of Parliament or Legislature. Exceptions for offices declared by Parliament not to be disqualifying.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disqualification for office under government under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: disqualification for office under government under RPA 1951

title: Filing of Nomination Papers
definition: Section 33 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Filing of Nomination Papers".
simplifiedExplanation: Candidate must file nomination with the Returning Officer. Must include: sworn affidavit with criminal cases, assets, liabilities, educational qualifications. Security deposit: ₹25,000 for Lok Sabha, ₹10,000 for Assembly.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to filing of nomination papers under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: filing of nomination papers under RPA 1951

title: Disclosure of Criminal Antecedents
definition: Section 33A of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disclosure of Criminal Antecedents".
simplifiedExplanation: Candidate must declare ALL criminal cases pending against them. Supreme Court mandated this disclosure so voters can make informed choices. Non-disclosure is ground for rejection of nomination.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disclosure of criminal antecedents under the RPA 1951.

importantCases.caseName: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India
importantCases.summary: Voters have right to know criminal records, assets, qualifications of candidates.

scenarioTags: disclosure of criminal antecedents under RPA 1951

title: Right to Vote
definition: Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Right to Vote".
simplifiedExplanation: Every person whose name appears in the electoral roll can vote. No person can vote more than once in the same constituency. No person can vote in more than one constituency. Voting is not compulsory (except in Gujarat local body elections).
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to vote under the RPA 1951.

title: Account of Election Expenses
definition: Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Account of Election Expenses".
simplifiedExplanation: Every candidate must keep a separate account of all election expenses. Lok Sabha limit: ₹95 lakh (most states) to ₹75 lakh. Assembly limit: ₹40 lakh (most states). Exceeding limit = corrupt practice.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to account of election expenses under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: account of election expenses under RPA 1951

title: Election Petition
definition: No election shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such High Court in accordance with the provisions of this Part.
simplifiedExplanation: If you want to challenge an election result — the ONLY way is to file an election petition in the High Court within 45 days of the result. No other court can hear election disputes. Election Tribunals within High Court hear these petitions.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to election petition under the RPA 1951.

title: Grounds for Declaring Election Void
definition: Section 100 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Grounds for Declaring Election Void".
simplifiedExplanation: Election is void if: (1) candidate was not qualified, (2) corrupt practice committed, (3) nomination improperly rejected, (4) result materially affected by non-compliance with election law, (5) votes improperly received/rejected.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to grounds for declaring election void under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: grounds for declaring election void under RPA 1951

title: Corrupt Practices
definition: The following shall be deemed corrupt practices: bribery, undue influence, appeal to vote on grounds of religion/race/caste/community/language, promoting enmity between classes, publication of false statements, hiring vehicles for voters, incurring expenditure beyond limit.
simplifiedExplanation: Corrupt practices include: (1) Bribery — giving money/gifts for votes, (2) Undue influence — threats/violence, (3) Communal appeal — asking to vote based on religion/caste, (4) False statements about rival's character, (5) Using government machinery, (6) Booth capturing.
punishment: Election declared void + possible criminal prosecution
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to corrupt practices under the RPA 1951.

importantCases.caseName: Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen
importantCases.summary: Appeal to vote on grounds of religion/caste of ANY candidate (not just the one making appeal) is corrupt practice under Section 123(3).

title: Promoting Enmity Between Classes
definition: Section 125 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Promoting Enmity Between Classes".
simplifiedExplanation: Anyone promoting enmity between classes of citizens on grounds of religion, race, caste, community, or language in connection with elections commits an offence punishable with imprisonment.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment or fine or both
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to promoting enmity between classes under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: promoting enmity between classes under RPA 1951

title: Prohibition of Electioneering During Certain Hours
definition: Section 126 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Prohibition of Electioneering During Certain Hours".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall display election matter, canvass, or distribute pamphlets during the period of 48 hours before the poll closes. Media cannot broadcast anything related to elections during this period.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of electioneering during certain hours under the RPA 1951.
tags: prohibition of electioneering during certain hours
aiSearchKeywords: prohibition of electioneering during certain hours
scenarioTags: prohibition of electioneering during certain hours under RPA 1951

title: Disturbances at Election Meetings
definition: Section 127 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Disturbances at Election Meetings".
simplifiedExplanation: Any person who causes disturbance at any public election meeting commits an offence. Right to peaceful assembly during elections is protected.
punishment: Up to 6 months imprisonment or fine of ₹2,000 or both
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disturbances at election meetings under the RPA 1951.
scenarioTags: disturbances at election meetings under RPA 1951

title: Prohibition of Canvassing Near Polling Station
definition: Section 130 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Prohibition of Canvassing Near Polling Station".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall canvass for votes or solicit votes within 100 meters of a polling station on the day of the poll. No candidate posters, flags, or party symbols within this zone.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of canvassing near polling station under the RPA 1951.
tags: prohibition of canvassing near polling station
aiSearchKeywords: prohibition of canvassing near polling station
scenarioTags: prohibition of canvassing near polling station under RPA 1951

title: Prohibition of Going Armed to Election
definition: Section 134B of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Prohibition of Going Armed to Election".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall go armed with any weapon near a polling station or at an election meeting. This includes licensed firearms — even licence holders cannot carry weapons near polling booths.
punishment: Up to 2 years imprisonment or fine or both
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of going armed to election under the RPA 1951.
tags: prohibition of going armed to election
aiSearchKeywords: prohibition of going armed to election
scenarioTags: prohibition of going armed to election under RPA 1951

title: Booth Capturing
definition: Booth capturing includes seizure of polling station, taking away ballot papers, threatening voters, seizure of counting place, threatening counting agents.
simplifiedExplanation: Booth capturing is one of the most serious election offences. If booth capturing affects the result, the election is declared void and re-polling is ordered. All results from captured booths are cancelled.
punishment: Minimum 1 year, up to 3 years imprisonment + fine
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to booth capturing under the RPA 1951.

title: Bribery in Elections
definition: Section 171B (IPC cross-reference) of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Bribery in Elections".
simplifiedExplanation: Giving or accepting gratification (money, liquor, food, gifts) to influence voting is bribery. Both the giver and receiver are punishable. 'Gratification' includes employment, property, or any favour.
punishment: Up to 1 year imprisonment or fine or both
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to bribery in elections under the RPA 1951.

title: Offences by Companies
definition: Section 136 of the Representation of the People Act 1951 deals with "Offences by Companies".
simplifiedExplanation: If election offences are committed by a company, every person who was in charge of the company at the time is personally liable. Directors can be prosecuted for company's election violations.
whoItAppliesTo: All candidates, parties, and voters in Indian elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offences by companies under the RPA 1951.

title: Recognition of Political Parties
definition: Para 6 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968 deals with "Recognition of Political Parties".
simplifiedExplanation: ECI recognizes parties as National or State parties based on vote share and seats won. National Party: 6% votes in 4+ states + 4 Lok Sabha seats OR 2% LS seats from 3+ states. State Party: 6% votes + 2 seats in state assembly.
whoItAppliesTo: Political parties and candidates contesting elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to recognition of political parties under the Symbols Order.

importantCases.caseName: Election Commission's Power to Recognize Parties
importantCases.summary: ECI has full power under Article 324 to recognize and derecognize political parties.
importantCases.significance: Upheld ECI's power over party recognition.

scenarioTags: recognition of political parties under Symbols Order

title: Reserved Symbols for Recognized Parties
definition: Para 7 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968 deals with "Reserved Symbols for Recognized Parties".
simplifiedExplanation: Recognized national and state parties get RESERVED symbols — no one else can use them. BJP's lotus, Congress's hand, BSP's elephant — these are reserved. Unrecognized parties get symbols from a free pool.
whoItAppliesTo: Political parties and candidates contesting elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to reserved symbols for recognized parties under the Symbols Order.
scenarioTags: reserved symbols for recognized parties under Symbols Order

title: Merger and Disputes About Symbols
definition: Para 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968 deals with "Merger and Disputes About Symbols".
simplifiedExplanation: When a party splits, ECI decides which faction gets the original party name and symbol. Factors considered: majority of organizational members, majority of legislators. This para was used in NCP and Shiv Sena splits.
whoItAppliesTo: Political parties and candidates contesting elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to merger and disputes about symbols under the Symbols Order.

importantCases.caseName: Sadiq Ali v. Election Commission
importantCases.summary: ECI has the final say in allotting symbols and deciding party splits under the Symbols Order.
importantCases.significance: Confirmed ECI's power to decide symbol disputes.

scenarioTags: merger and disputes about symbols under Symbols Order

title: Conditions for Continued Recognition
definition: Para 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968 deals with "Conditions for Continued Recognition".
simplifiedExplanation: A party must maintain minimum vote share and seat thresholds to retain recognition. If a national party fails to get 6% votes in 4 states in successive elections, it can lose national party status.
whoItAppliesTo: Political parties and candidates contesting elections
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to conditions for continued recognition under the Symbols Order.
scenarioTags: conditions for continued recognition under Symbols Order

title: Works in Which Copyright Subsists
definition: Section 13 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Works in Which Copyright Subsists".
simplifiedExplanation: Copyright protection exists in: (1) literary works (books, software), (2) dramatic works (scripts, plays), (3) musical works (compositions), (4) artistic works (paintings, photographs, architecture), (5) cinematograph films, (6) sound recordings. NO registration needed — copyright is automatic.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to works in which copyright subsists under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: works in which copyright subsists under Copyright Act

title: Meaning of Copyright
definition: Section 14 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Meaning of Copyright".
simplifiedExplanation: Copyright = exclusive right to: (1) reproduce the work, (2) issue copies to public, (3) perform in public, (4) communicate to public, (5) make translations, (6) make adaptations. For software: right to sell or give on commercial rental.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to meaning of copyright under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: meaning of copyright under Copyright Act

title: First Owner of Copyright
definition: Section 17 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "First Owner of Copyright".
simplifiedExplanation: Author is the first owner of copyright. EXCEPTION: if work is created during employment — employer owns copyright. If work is created under contract — person who contracted owns it. Government owns copyright of government works.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to first owner of copyright under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: first owner of copyright under Copyright Act

title: Term of Copyright — Literary, Dramatic, Musical, Artistic
definition: Section 22 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Term of Copyright — Literary, Dramatic, Musical, Artistic".
simplifiedExplanation: Copyright lasts for: lifetime of author + 60 years after death. For anonymous/pseudonymous: 60 years from publication. For government/public undertaking: 60 years from publication. For photographs: 60 years from publication.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to term of copyright — literary, dramatic, musical, artistic under the Copyright Act.
tags: term of copyright — literary, dramatic, musical, artistic
aiSearchKeywords: term of copyright — literary, dramatic, musical, artistic
scenarioTags: term of copyright — literary, dramatic, musical, artistic under Copyright Act

title: Term of Copyright in Films
definition: Section 26 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Term of Copyright in Films".
simplifiedExplanation: Copyright in cinematograph films: 60 years from year of publication. The producer (not director) is the first owner of copyright in films.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to term of copyright in films under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: term of copyright in films under Copyright Act

title: Assignment of Copyright
definition: Section 30 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Assignment of Copyright".
simplifiedExplanation: Copyright can be assigned (sold/transferred) wholly or partly. Assignment must be in writing signed by assignor. Cannot assign future works or for more than 5 years at a time (can be renewed). Author has right to renegotiate after 5 years.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to assignment of copyright under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: assignment of copyright under Copyright Act

title: Registration of Copyright
definition: Section 33 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Registration of Copyright".
simplifiedExplanation: Registration of copyright is optional — copyright exists automatically upon creation. But registration creates a presumption of ownership and is useful evidence in court.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to registration of copyright under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: registration of copyright under Copyright Act

title: When Copyright Is Infringed
definition: Copyright is infringed when any person, without licence of the copyright owner, does anything which the copyright owner has the exclusive right to do.
simplifiedExplanation: Infringement includes: copying, distributing pirated copies, performing in public without permission, making unauthorized adaptations. Importing pirated copies is also infringement.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to when copyright is infringed under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: when copyright is infringed under Copyright Act

title: Fair Dealing — Fair Use
definition: Section 52 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Fair Dealing — Fair Use".
simplifiedExplanation: Fair dealing is NOT infringement. You can: (1) use for private study/research, (2) criticism or review, (3) reporting current events, (4) judicial proceedings, (5) parody, (6) educational purposes (classroom teaching), (7) back-up copies of software.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to fair dealing — fair use under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: fair dealing — fair use under Copyright Act

title: Author's Special Rights — Moral Rights
definition: Section 57 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Author's Special Rights — Moral Rights".
simplifiedExplanation: Even after assigning copyright, the author retains: (1) right to claim authorship (paternity right), (2) right to prevent distortion, mutilation, or modification of the work (integrity right). These rights are perpetual and cannot be assigned.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to author's special rights — moral rights under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: author's special rights — moral rights under Copyright Act

title: Offence of Infringement of Copyright
definition: Section 63 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Offence of Infringement of Copyright".
simplifiedExplanation: Knowingly infringing copyright is a criminal offence. Both civil suit for damages AND criminal prosecution are possible. Police can seize pirated copies without warrant.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offence of infringement of copyright under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: offence of infringement of copyright under Copyright Act

title: Possession of Infringing Copies
definition: Section 65 of the Copyright Act 1957 deals with "Possession of Infringing Copies".
simplifiedExplanation: Possessing plates or copies used for making pirated copies is itself an offence. Even if you haven't sold them — just possessing them for commercial purpose is punishable.
whoItAppliesTo: Authors, artists, creators, publishers, broadcasters
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to possession of infringing copies under the Copyright Act.
scenarioTags: possession of infringing copies under Copyright Act

title: Invention Defined
definition: Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Invention Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Invention means a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application. Three requirements: (1) Novelty — new, (2) Inventive Step — non-obvious, (3) Industrial Application — useful.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to invention defined under the Patents Act.

title: What Are Not Inventions
definition: Section 3 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "What Are Not Inventions".
simplifiedExplanation: NOT patentable: (1) discovery of natural things, (2) mathematical methods, (3) business methods, (4) computer programs per se, (5) plants and animals, (6) traditional knowledge, (7) inventions contrary to morality, (8) methods of agriculture. Section 3(d): mere new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy NOT patentable.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to what are not inventions under the Patents Act.

importantCases.caseName: Novartis v. Union of India
importantCases.summary: Novartis denied patent for Glivec — a modified form of known substance without enhanced therapeutic efficacy. Section 3(d) upheld.
importantCases.significance: Most important Indian patent case. Upheld India's strict patentability standards.

scenarioTags: what are not inventions under Patents Act

title: Inventions Relating to Atomic Energy — Not Patentable
definition: Section 5 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Inventions Relating to Atomic Energy — Not Patentable".
simplifiedExplanation: No patent can be granted for inventions relating to atomic energy under Atomic Energy Act 1962. All nuclear technology is controlled by the government.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to inventions relating to atomic energy — not patentable under the Patents Act.
tags: inventions relating to atomic energy — not patentable
aiSearchKeywords: inventions relating to atomic energy — not patentable
scenarioTags: inventions relating to atomic energy — not patentable under Patents Act

title: Application for Patent
definition: Section 6 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Application for Patent".
simplifiedExplanation: Patent application must be filed at the Patent Office. Can be filed by: true inventor, assignee, or legal representative. Application must include: specification, claims, abstract, drawings. Provisional specification can be filed first.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to application for patent under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: application for patent under Patents Act

title: Contents of Patent Specification
definition: Section 10 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Contents of Patent Specification".
simplifiedExplanation: Complete specification must: (1) fully describe the invention so anyone skilled in the art can make it, (2) disclose the best method of performing it, (3) end with claims defining the scope of protection. Claims are the most important part.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to contents of patent specification under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: contents of patent specification under Patents Act

title: Opposition to Grant of Patent — Pre-Grant
definition: Section 25(1) of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Opposition to Grant of Patent — Pre-Grant".
simplifiedExplanation: Any person can oppose grant of patent within 6 months of publication of application. Grounds: not novel, obvious, not useful, not an invention under Section 3, wrong person claiming, prior publication, etc.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to opposition to grant of patent — pre-grant under the Patents Act.
tags: opposition to grant of patent — pre-grant
aiSearchKeywords: opposition to grant of patent — pre-grant
scenarioTags: opposition to grant of patent — pre-grant under Patents Act

title: Opposition After Grant — Post-Grant
definition: Section 25(2) of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Opposition After Grant — Post-Grant".
simplifiedExplanation: After patent is granted, any interested person can oppose it within 1 year. Same grounds as pre-grant opposition. This is a second chance to challenge a wrongly granted patent.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to opposition after grant — post-grant under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: opposition after grant — post-grant under Patents Act

title: Rights of Patentee
definition: Section 48 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Rights of Patentee".
simplifiedExplanation: Patent holder has exclusive right to: (1) for products — make, use, sell, import the patented product, (2) for processes — use the process and sell products made by the process. Patent term: 20 years from date of filing.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to rights of patentee under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: rights of patentee under Patents Act

title: Compulsory Licensing
definition: At any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the grant of a patent, any person interested may make an application for compulsory licence on grounds that reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied.
simplifiedExplanation: If a patent holder does not make the invention available to public at reasonable price, anyone can apply for compulsory licence — forced licence to manufacture. India granted compulsory licence to Natco Pharma for Nexavar (cancer drug) in 2012.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to compulsory licensing under the Patents Act.

importantCases.caseName: Natco Pharma v. Bayer Corporation
importantCases.summary: India's first compulsory licence granted — Natco allowed to make generic Nexavar (cancer drug) at 3% of Bayer's price.
importantCases.significance: First compulsory licence in India. Made cancer drugs affordable.

title: Compulsory Licence During National Emergency
definition: Section 92 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Compulsory Licence During National Emergency".
simplifiedExplanation: During national emergency, epidemic, or extreme urgency — the Controller can grant compulsory licence without the usual 3-year waiting period. This was invoked during COVID-19 discussions.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to compulsory licence during national emergency under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: compulsory licence during national emergency under Patents Act

title: Defences to Patent Infringement
definition: Section 107 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Defences to Patent Infringement".
simplifiedExplanation: Defences: (1) patent is invalid, (2) prior use — using before patent was filed, (3) experimental use, (4) parallel import — legally bought from patentee in another country, (5) Bolar exception — testing for regulatory approval of generic drug.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to defences to patent infringement under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: defences to patent infringement under Patents Act

title: Secrecy of Certain Inventions
definition: Section 118 of the Patents Act 1970 deals with "Secrecy of Certain Inventions".
simplifiedExplanation: Inventions relevant to defence or national security may be kept secret by direction of the Controller. Patent application is restricted and publication is prohibited.
whoItAppliesTo: Inventors, patent holders, companies, researchers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to secrecy of certain inventions under the Patents Act.
scenarioTags: secrecy of certain inventions under Patents Act

title: Trade Mark Defined
definition: Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Trade Mark Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: A trade mark is a mark capable of graphical representation that distinguishes goods/services of one person from others. Includes: words, letters, numerals, designs, logos, shapes, colours, sounds. Must be distinctive.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to trade mark defined under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: trade mark defined under Trade Marks Act

title: Absolute Grounds for Refusal
definition: Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Absolute Grounds for Refusal".
simplifiedExplanation: Cannot register marks that: (1) lack distinctive character, (2) are descriptive of goods/services, (3) are customary in trade, (4) are deceptive, (5) contain scandalous matter, (6) are prohibited under Emblem and Names Act.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to absolute grounds for refusal under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: absolute grounds for refusal under Trade Marks Act

title: Relative Grounds for Refusal
definition: Section 11 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Relative Grounds for Refusal".
simplifiedExplanation: Cannot register mark if it is: (1) identical to an earlier mark for same goods/services, (2) similar to earlier mark and likely to cause confusion, (3) identical/similar to a well-known mark.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to relative grounds for refusal under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: relative grounds for refusal under Trade Marks Act

title: Opposition to Registration
definition: Section 21 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Opposition to Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Any person can oppose a trademark registration within 4 months of publication in Trade Marks Journal. Grounds: earlier mark exists, mark is descriptive, mark is deceptive, bad faith application.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to opposition to registration under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: opposition to registration under Trade Marks Act

title: Effect of Registration
definition: Section 27 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Effect of Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Registration gives exclusive right to use the mark for the registered goods/services. Registered mark is prima facie evidence of validity. Unregistered marks can be protected under 'passing off' common law.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to effect of registration under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: effect of registration under Trade Marks Act

title: Infringement of Trade Mark
definition: Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Infringement of Trade Mark".
simplifiedExplanation: Infringement = using identical/similar mark for identical/similar goods without permission. Even using a mark as a trade name or domain name can be infringement. Well-known marks are protected even for different goods.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to infringement of trade mark under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: infringement of trade mark under Trade Marks Act

title: Limits on Effect of Registration — Fair Use
definition: Section 30 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Limits on Effect of Registration — Fair Use".
simplifiedExplanation: Using a registered mark is NOT infringement if: (1) honest use of own name, (2) descriptive use, (3) indicating intended purpose of goods, (4) use by registered user, (5) comparative advertising in honest manner.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to limits on effect of registration — fair use under the Trade Marks Act.
tags: limits on effect of registration — fair use
aiSearchKeywords: limits on effect of registration — fair use
scenarioTags: limits on effect of registration — fair use under Trade Marks Act

title: Removal of Trade Mark for Non-Use
definition: Section 47 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Removal of Trade Mark for Non-Use".
simplifiedExplanation: If a trademark is not used for 5 years, any person can apply for its removal from the register. The burden is on the trademark owner to prove use. This prevents trademark hoarding.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to removal of trade mark for non-use under the Trade Marks Act.
tags: removal of trade mark for non-use
aiSearchKeywords: removal of trade mark for non-use
scenarioTags: removal of trade mark for non-use under Trade Marks Act

title: Penalty for Using False Trade Mark
definition: Section 103 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Penalty for Using False Trade Mark".
simplifiedExplanation: Selling goods with a false trademark (counterfeiting) is a criminal offence. Police can raid and seize counterfeit goods. Both the manufacturer and seller are liable.
punishment: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for using false trade mark under the Trade Marks Act.
tags: penalty for using false trade mark
aiSearchKeywords: penalty for using false trade mark
scenarioTags: penalty for using false trade mark under Trade Marks Act

title: Jurisdiction — Where to Sue
definition: Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act 1999 deals with "Jurisdiction — Where to Sue".
simplifiedExplanation: Trademark infringement suit can be filed where the plaintiff resides or carries on business — NOT necessarily where the defendant is. This is a plaintiff-friendly provision unique to trademark law.
whoItAppliesTo: Business owners, companies, brand owners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to jurisdiction — where to sue under the Trade Marks Act.
scenarioTags: jurisdiction — where to sue under Trade Marks Act

title: Design Defined
definition: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act 2000 deals with "Design Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Design means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines/colours applied to any article by any industrial process. Only visual appearance is protected — NOT the function.
whoItAppliesTo: Designers, manufacturers, product companies
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to design defined under the Designs Act.

title: Prohibition of Registration of Certain Designs
definition: Section 4 of the Designs Act 2000 deals with "Prohibition of Registration of Certain Designs".
simplifiedExplanation: Cannot register designs that are: (1) not new or original, (2) published in India before, (3) not significantly distinguishable from known designs, (4) scandalous or obscene.
whoItAppliesTo: Designers, manufacturers, product companies
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of registration of certain designs under the Designs Act.
tags: prohibition of registration of certain designs
aiSearchKeywords: prohibition of registration of certain designs
scenarioTags: prohibition of registration of certain designs under Designs Act

title: Copyright on Registration
definition: Section 11 of the Designs Act 2000 deals with "Copyright on Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Registration gives exclusive right to apply the design to the article for 10 years (extendable by 5 years, total 15 years). During this period, no one else can copy the design without permission.
whoItAppliesTo: Designers, manufacturers, product companies
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to copyright on registration under the Designs Act.
scenarioTags: copyright on registration under Designs Act

title: Piracy of Registered Design
definition: Section 22 of the Designs Act 2000 deals with "Piracy of Registered Design".
simplifiedExplanation: Copying a registered design is 'piracy of design'. The design owner can sue for damages or get injunction. Can also seek account of profits made by the infringer.
punishment: Up to ₹50,000 for each offence (civil). Contract price for each article if suit filed.
whoItAppliesTo: Designers, manufacturers, product companies
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to piracy of registered design under the Designs Act.
scenarioTags: piracy of registered design under Designs Act

lawName: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
title: Geographical Indication Defined
definition: Section 1(3)(e) of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 deals with "Geographical Indication Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: A GI identifies goods as originating from a specific region where its quality, reputation, or characteristics are essentially attributable to its geographical origin. Examples: Darjeeling Tea, Banarasi Saree, Tirupati Laddu, Champagne.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, associations of goods associated with specific geographical origins
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to geographical indication defined under the GI Act.
scenarioTags: geographical indication defined under GI Act

lawName: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
title: Application for Registration of GI
definition: Section 6 of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 deals with "Application for Registration of GI".
simplifiedExplanation: Any association of persons, producers, organization, or authority can apply for GI registration. Individual persons CANNOT register a GI — it belongs to the community/region.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, associations of goods associated with specific geographical origins
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to application for registration of gi under the GI Act.
scenarioTags: application for registration of gi under GI Act

lawName: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
title: Duration and Renewal
definition: Section 17 of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 deals with "Duration and Renewal".
simplifiedExplanation: GI registration is valid for 10 years and can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods. GI never expires as long as it is renewed.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, associations of goods associated with specific geographical origins
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to duration and renewal under the GI Act.
scenarioTags: duration and renewal under GI Act

lawName: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
title: Infringement of GI
definition: Section 21 of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 deals with "Infringement of GI".
simplifiedExplanation: Using a registered GI on goods not originating from that geographical area is infringement. Even using 'style', 'type', 'like' (e.g., 'Darjeeling-style tea') is infringement.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, associations of goods associated with specific geographical origins
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to infringement of gi under the GI Act.
scenarioTags: infringement of gi under GI Act

lawName: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
title: Permitted Use of GI
definition: Section 22 of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 deals with "Permitted Use of GI".
simplifiedExplanation: A registered GI can be used by any authorized user from that geographical area. The GI is a community right — it cannot be assigned or licensed to outsiders.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, associations of goods associated with specific geographical origins
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to permitted use of gi under the GI Act.
scenarioTags: permitted use of gi under GI Act

title: Banking Defined
definition: Banking means the accepting, for the purpose of lending or investment, of deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise.
simplifiedExplanation: Banking = accepting deposits from public for lending/investment + allowing withdrawal by cheque. This is what distinguishes banks from other financial institutions. Without RBI licence, no entity can do banking.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to banking defined under the BR Act.

title: Forms of Business in Which Banking Companies May Engage
definition: Section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Forms of Business in Which Banking Companies May Engage".
simplifiedExplanation: Banks can: accept deposits, give loans, buy/sell/deal in bills of exchange, deal in foreign exchange, act as agents, provide safe custody, deal in gold/silver. Banks CANNOT engage in trading of goods (with some exceptions).
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to forms of business in which banking companies may engage under the BR Act.
tags: forms of business in which banking companies may engage
aiSearchKeywords: forms of business in which banking companies may engage
scenarioTags: forms of business in which banking companies may engage under BR Act

title: Requirement as to Minimum Paid-Up Capital
definition: Section 11 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Requirement as to Minimum Paid-Up Capital".
simplifiedExplanation: Minimum capital requirements for banking companies. Currently ₹500 crore for new banks. Foreign banks must maintain minimum capital as prescribed by RBI.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to requirement as to minimum paid-up capital under the BR Act.
tags: requirement as to minimum paid-up capital
aiSearchKeywords: requirement as to minimum paid-up capital
scenarioTags: requirement as to minimum paid-up capital under BR Act

title: Cash Reserve — CRR
definition: Section 18 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Cash Reserve — CRR".
simplifiedExplanation: Every bank must maintain a minimum Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) with RBI. Currently around 4-4.5% of net demand and time liabilities. This money earns no interest. RBI uses CRR to control money supply.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to cash reserve — crr under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: cash reserve — crr under BR Act

title: Power of RBI to Control Advances
definition: Section 21 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Power of RBI to Control Advances".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI can direct banks on: (1) purposes for which loans can/cannot be given, (2) margins to be maintained, (3) maximum amount of loan to any borrower, (4) rate of interest. This is how RBI controls credit in the economy.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power of rbi to control advances under the BR Act.
tags: power of rbi to control advances
aiSearchKeywords: power of rbi to control advances
scenarioTags: power of rbi to control advances under BR Act

title: Licensing of Banking Companies
definition: Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Licensing of Banking Companies".
simplifiedExplanation: No company can carry on banking business without a licence from RBI. RBI can cancel licence if bank is unable to pay debts or has contravened this Act. Cancelled licence = bank must stop all operations.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to licensing of banking companies under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: licensing of banking companies under BR Act

title: Statutory Liquidity Ratio — SLR
definition: Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Statutory Liquidity Ratio — SLR".
simplifiedExplanation: Every bank must maintain a minimum percentage (SLR) of its demand and time liabilities in liquid assets — government securities, cash, gold. Currently around 18%. This ensures banks always have enough liquid assets.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to statutory liquidity ratio — slr under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: statutory liquidity ratio — slr under BR Act

title: Power of RBI to Give Directions
definition: Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Power of RBI to Give Directions".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI can give directions to any banking company in the interest of depositors, banking policy, or public interest. Banks MUST comply. Non-compliance: up to ₹50 lakh penalty.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power of rbi to give directions under the BR Act.
tags: power of rbi to give directions
aiSearchKeywords: power of rbi to give directions
scenarioTags: power of rbi to give directions under BR Act

title: Moratorium and Merger
definition: Section 36AD of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Moratorium and Merger".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI can impose moratorium on a bank (freeze all activities for up to 6 months) if the bank's financial position has deteriorated. During moratorium, RBI prepares a scheme of reconstruction or merger.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to moratorium and merger under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: moratorium and merger under BR Act

title: Winding Up of Banking Company
definition: Section 44 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Winding Up of Banking Company".
simplifiedExplanation: High Court can order winding up of a bank on application by RBI. RBI's opinion that bank cannot pay debts is prima facie evidence. Depositors are first in priority of payments.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to winding up of banking company under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: winding up of banking company under BR Act

title: Power of RBI to Apply for Winding Up
definition: Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Power of RBI to Apply for Winding Up".
