simplifiedExplanation: Only RBI can apply for winding up of a banking company. No other person or institution can file for winding up of a bank. This centralizes banking regulation.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power of rbi to apply for winding up under the BR Act.
tags: power of rbi to apply for winding up
aiSearchKeywords: power of rbi to apply for winding up
scenarioTags: power of rbi to apply for winding up under BR Act

title: Application to Co-operative Banks
definition: Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 deals with "Application to Co-operative Banks".
simplifiedExplanation: Part V of BR Act applies to cooperative banks with modifications. RBI has regulatory powers over cooperative banks similar to commercial banks. Urban cooperative banks are directly under RBI since 2020.
whoItAppliesTo: All banking companies, cooperative banks, RBI
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to application to co-operative banks under the BR Act.
scenarioTags: application to co-operative banks under BR Act

title: Establishment of RBI
definition: Section 3 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Establishment of RBI".
simplifiedExplanation: Reserve Bank of India was established on April 1, 1935. Originally a private shareholders' bank, it was nationalized in 1949. Headquarters: Mumbai.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to establishment of rbi under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: establishment of rbi under RBI Act

title: Management of RBI
definition: Section 7 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Management of RBI".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI is managed by a Central Board of Directors: Governor (appointed by Government), 4 Deputy Governors, 4 directors nominated by government, and others. Governor's term: usually 3 years.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to management of rbi under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: management of rbi under RBI Act

title: Business Which RBI May Transact
definition: Section 17 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Business Which RBI May Transact".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI can: accept deposits from central/state governments, banks. Buy/sell/rediscount bills. Deal in foreign exchange. Grant loans to central/state governments. Buy/sell government securities.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to business which rbi may transact under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: business which rbi may transact under RBI Act

title: Right to Issue Bank Notes
definition: Section 22 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Right to Issue Bank Notes".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI has the sole right to issue bank notes in India. ₹1 note is issued by Government of India (Ministry of Finance), all others by RBI. Notes are printed at 4 printing presses.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to issue bank notes under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: right to issue bank notes under RBI Act

title: Denomination of Notes
definition: Section 24 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Denomination of Notes".
simplifiedExplanation: RBI can issue notes in denominations of ₹2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 2000. The ₹2000 note was introduced in 2016 after demonetization. Central Government decides denominations.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to denomination of notes under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: denomination of notes under RBI Act

title: Legal Tender Character of Notes
definition: Section 26 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Legal Tender Character of Notes".
simplifiedExplanation: Every bank note issued by RBI is legal tender. This means it must be accepted for payment of any amount. 'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of...' on every note.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to legal tender character of notes under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: legal tender character of notes under RBI Act

title: Demonetization of Bank Notes
definition: Section 28 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Demonetization of Bank Notes".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can declare any denomination of bank note to cease to be legal tender. This was used on November 8, 2016 to demonetize ₹500 and ₹1000 notes.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to demonetization of bank notes under the RBI Act.

importantCases.caseName: Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India
importantCases.summary: Demonetization of ₹500 and ₹1000 notes upheld as valid. 4:1 majority. Decision-making process was not unreasonable.
importantCases.significance: Upheld government's power to demonetize currency.

scenarioTags: demonetization of bank notes under RBI Act

title: Scheduled Banks — Cash Reserve
definition: Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Scheduled Banks — Cash Reserve".
simplifiedExplanation: Every scheduled bank must maintain average daily CRR with RBI. RBI can vary CRR between 3% and 15% of total demand and time liabilities. This is a key monetary policy tool.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to scheduled banks — cash reserve under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: scheduled banks — cash reserve under RBI Act

title: Monetary Policy Committee — MPC
definition: Section 45ZA of the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 deals with "Monetary Policy Committee — MPC".
simplifiedExplanation: MPC was established in 2016 by amending RBI Act. 6 members: 3 from RBI (including Governor as chair) + 3 external members appointed by Government. MPC decides repo rate. Decision by majority vote. Governor has casting vote.
whoItAppliesTo: Reserve Bank of India and all scheduled banks
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to monetary policy committee — mpc under the RBI Act.
scenarioTags: monetary policy committee — mpc under RBI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Notice to Borrower — 60-Day Demand Notice
definition: Section 13(2) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Notice to Borrower — 60-Day Demand Notice".
simplifiedExplanation: When a borrower defaults on a secured loan (loan becomes NPA), the bank can issue a 60-day demand notice requiring the borrower to pay the outstanding amount. If not paid within 60 days, bank can take action WITHOUT going to court.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to notice to borrower — 60-day demand notice under the SARFAESI Act.
scenarioTags: notice to borrower — 60-day demand notice under SARFAESI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Measures After 60-Day Notice
definition: Section 13(4) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Measures After 60-Day Notice".
simplifiedExplanation: After 60 days, bank can: (1) take possession of the secured asset, (2) sell the asset, (3) take over management of the borrower's business, (4) appoint any person to manage the asset. This is done WITHOUT court intervention.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to measures after 60-day notice under the SARFAESI Act.
scenarioTags: measures after 60-day notice under SARFAESI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Chief Metropolitan Magistrate to Assist in Taking Possession
definition: Section 14 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Chief Metropolitan Magistrate to Assist in Taking Possession".
simplifiedExplanation: If borrower does not cooperate in handing over property, bank can approach the CMM/District Magistrate who MUST assist in taking possession. DM must pass order within 30 days.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to chief metropolitan magistrate to assist in taking possession under the SARFAESI Act.
tags: chief metropolitan magistrate to assist in taking possession
aiSearchKeywords: chief metropolitan magistrate to assist in taking possession
scenarioTags: chief metropolitan magistrate to assist in taking possession under SARFAESI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Right of Borrower — Appeal to DRT
definition: Section 17 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Right of Borrower — Appeal to DRT".
simplifiedExplanation: Borrower can appeal SARFAESI action to Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) within 45 days of action taken. DRT must dispose within 60 days. DRT can set aside bank's action if it was not in accordance with law.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right of borrower — appeal to drt under the SARFAESI Act.
tags: right of borrower — appeal to drt
aiSearchKeywords: right of borrower — appeal to drt
scenarioTags: right of borrower — appeal to drt under SARFAESI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Appeal to DRAT
definition: Section 18 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Appeal to DRAT".
simplifiedExplanation: Appeal against DRT's order lies to Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within 30 days. Borrower must deposit 50% of debt (or as DRAT directs) to file appeal.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to appeal to drat under the SARFAESI Act.
scenarioTags: appeal to drat under SARFAESI Act

lawName: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002
title: Priority of Secured Creditors
definition: Section 26E of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act 2002 deals with "Priority of Secured Creditors".
simplifiedExplanation: In case of liquidation, secured creditors (banks) have FIRST priority over government dues (tax dues). Only worker's wages for 24 months have higher priority than banks.
whoItAppliesTo: Banks, financial institutions, and borrowers who default on secured loans
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to priority of secured creditors under the SARFAESI Act.

importantCases.caseName: Central Bank of India v. State of Kerala
importantCases.summary: Secured creditors have priority over state government's tax dues in recovery proceedings.
importantCases.significance: Established priority of banks in NPA recovery.

scenarioTags: priority of secured creditors under SARFAESI Act

title: Human Rights Defined
definition: Section 2(d) of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Human Rights Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Human rights means rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity of the individual guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by courts in India.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to human rights defined under the PHRA.

title: Constitution of NHRC
definition: Section 3 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Constitution of NHRC".
simplifiedExplanation: NHRC consists of: Chairperson (retired CJI), 1 member who is/was SC judge, 1 member who is/was HC CJ, 2 members with knowledge of human rights. After 2019 amendment: Chairperson can also be a former SC judge.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to constitution of nhrc under the PHRA.

title: Functions of NHRC
definition: Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Functions of NHRC".
simplifiedExplanation: NHRC can: (1) inquire into violation of human rights by state, (2) intervene in court proceedings, (3) visit jails for conditions, (4) review laws and recommend changes, (5) study international treaties and recommend implementation, (6) promote human rights literacy.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to functions of nhrc under the PHRA.

title: Powers of NHRC
definition: Section 13 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Powers of NHRC".
simplifiedExplanation: NHRC has powers of a civil court: can summon witnesses, compel production of documents, receive evidence on affidavit. But it is only a RECOMMENDATORY body — it cannot enforce its decisions. Government must respond to recommendations within 1 month.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to powers of nhrc under the PHRA.

title: Steps After NHRC Inquiry
definition: Section 18 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Steps After NHRC Inquiry".
simplifiedExplanation: After inquiry, NHRC can: (1) recommend prosecution, (2) recommend compensation, (3) approach Supreme Court/High Court for directions. NHRC cannot itself prosecute or award compensation — it can only recommend.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to steps after nhrc inquiry under the PHRA.
scenarioTags: steps after nhrc inquiry under PHRA

title: State Human Rights Commission — SHRC
definition: Section 21 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "State Human Rights Commission — SHRC".
simplifiedExplanation: Every state can constitute a State Human Rights Commission. Chairperson: retired HC CJ. Functions similar to NHRC but for state-level violations.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to state human rights commission — shrc under the PHRA.
scenarioTags: state human rights commission — shrc under PHRA

title: Human Rights Courts
definition: Section 24 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "Human Rights Courts".
simplifiedExplanation: State Government must specify a Sessions Court as Human Rights Court in each district for speedy trial of human rights offences. Each court must have a Special Public Prosecutor.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to human rights courts under the PHRA.

title: NHRC Cannot Inquire into Armed Forces Matters
definition: Section 30 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 deals with "NHRC Cannot Inquire into Armed Forces Matters".
simplifiedExplanation: NHRC cannot inquire into complaints against armed forces. It can only seek a report from the Central Government. This is a major limitation — human rights violations by army (e.g., in AFSPA areas) cannot be directly investigated by NHRC.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to nhrc cannot inquire into armed forces matters under the PHRA.
tags: nhrc cannot inquire into armed forces matters
aiSearchKeywords: nhrc cannot inquire into armed forces matters
scenarioTags: nhrc cannot inquire into armed forces matters under PHRA

lawName: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
title: Offences of Atrocities
definition: Section 3(1) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 deals with "Offences of Atrocities".
simplifiedExplanation: Atrocities against SC/ST include: (i) forcing to eat/drink inedible substances, (ii) dumping waste on their property, (iii) removing clothes/parading naked, (iv) wrongfully occupying their land, (v) compelling to do bonded labour, (vi) intimidating during voting, (vii) preventing from entering public places, (viii) making false criminal case against SC/ST person.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons — offences against SC/ST members
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offences of atrocities under the SC/ST Act.

simplifiedExplanation: Victims and witnesses have the right to: (1) reasonable treatment, (2) protection from intimidation, (3) right to be informed of proceedings, (4) free legal aid, (5) travel expenses for attending court.
punishment: 6 months to 5 years + fine (enhanced for certain offences)

title: Presumption as to Offence
definition: Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 deals with "Presumption as to Offence".
simplifiedExplanation: Court shall presume that accused committed the offence unless contrary is proved. This reverses the burden of proof — accused must prove innocence. Very unusual in criminal law.
punishment: 6 months to 5 years + fine (enhanced for certain offences)
whoItAppliesTo: All persons — offences against SC/ST members

lawName: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016
title: Reservation in Employment

title: Bonded Labour System Defined
definition: Section 2(g) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "Bonded Labour System Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Bonded labour system means any system of forced labour where a person provides labour or service to a creditor in consideration of an advance (loan) or obligation and is not free to leave.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to bonded labour system defined under the Bonded Labour Act.
scenarioTags: bonded labour system defined under Bonded Labour Act

title: Abolition of Bonded Labour System
definition: Section 4 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "Abolition of Bonded Labour System".
simplifiedExplanation: On the commencement of this Act, the bonded labour system shall be abolished and every bonded labourer shall stand freed and discharged from any obligation to render bonded labour. ALL existing bonded labour agreements are VOID.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to abolition of bonded labour system under the Bonded Labour Act.
scenarioTags: abolition of bonded labour system under Bonded Labour Act

title: Liability to Repay Bonded Debt Extinguished
definition: Section 6 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "Liability to Repay Bonded Debt Extinguished".
simplifiedExplanation: The bonded labourer is NOT required to repay the debt for which they were bonded. The debt is extinguished by law. Even if they actually owe money, the bonded labour agreement is void.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to liability to repay bonded debt extinguished under the Bonded Labour Act.

title: District Magistrate's Duty
definition: Section 10 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "District Magistrate's Duty".
simplifiedExplanation: The DM must: (1) inquire whether bonded labour exists in the district, (2) release bonded labourers, (3) provide economic rehabilitation, (4) allot house-site and agricultural land. DM has direct responsibility.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to district magistrate's duty under the Bonded Labour Act.
scenarioTags: district magistrate's duty under Bonded Labour Act

title: Punishment for Enforcing Bonded Labour
definition: Section 16 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "Punishment for Enforcing Bonded Labour".
simplifiedExplanation: Any person who forces someone to work as bonded labour is punishable. This includes advancing money knowing the debtor will be forced to work to repay.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to punishment for enforcing bonded labour under the Bonded Labour Act.
scenarioTags: punishment for enforcing bonded labour under Bonded Labour Act

title: Punishment for Extracting Bonded Labour Under System
definition: Section 18 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 deals with "Punishment for Extracting Bonded Labour Under System".
simplifiedExplanation: Extracting bonded labour from any person under the bonded labour system is punishable even if the system existed before the Act. There is no grandfather clause.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors

simplifiedExplanation: District and Sub-Divisional Vigilance Committees must be constituted to: advise the DM, provide assistance in implementation, identify and rehabilitate bonded labourers. Must include 3 members from SC/ST communities.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to ₹2,000
whoItAppliesTo: All bonded labourers and their families, employers, creditors

title: Constitution of National Medical Commission
definition: Section 3 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "Constitution of National Medical Commission".
simplifiedExplanation: NMC replaces the Medical Council of India (MCI). It has 33 members including chairperson. NMC regulates medical education, medical practice, and medical institutions across India.
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to constitution of national medical commission under the NMC Act.

title: Autonomous Boards Under NMC
definition: Section 10 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "Autonomous Boards Under NMC".
simplifiedExplanation: NMC has 4 autonomous boards: (1) Under-Graduate Medical Education Board, (2) Post-Graduate Medical Education Board, (3) Medical Assessment and Rating Board, (4) Ethics and Medical Registration Board.
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to autonomous boards under nmc under the NMC Act.

title: Permission for New Medical Colleges
definition: Section 15 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "Permission for New Medical Colleges".
simplifiedExplanation: Prior permission of Medical Assessment and Rating Board is required to establish a new medical college, start new courses, or increase admission capacity. Without permission — recognition will not be granted.
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to permission for new medical colleges under the NMC Act.

title: National Register of Medical Practitioners
definition: Section 24 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "National Register of Medical Practitioners".
simplifiedExplanation: A National Register is maintained listing all registered medical practitioners in India. Only persons on this register can practice modern medicine. State Medical Councils maintain State Registers.
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to national register of medical practitioners under the NMC Act.
scenarioTags: national register of medical practitioners under NMC Act

title: Right to Practice Medicine
definition: Section 28 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "Right to Practice Medicine".
simplifiedExplanation: Only a person with recognized medical qualification and registered in the National/State Register can practice medicine. Practicing without registration is punishable with up to 1 year imprisonment.
punishment: Up to 1 year imprisonment + up to ₹5 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to practice medicine under the NMC Act.
scenarioTags: right to practice medicine under NMC Act

title: NEXT — National Exit Test
definition: Section 32 of the National Medical Commission Act 2019 deals with "NEXT — National Exit Test".
simplifiedExplanation: NEXT is a common final-year MBBS examination that will serve as: (1) licentiate exam to practice medicine, (2) postgraduate entrance exam (replacing NEET-PG), (3) screening test for foreign medical graduates.
whoItAppliesTo: Medical practitioners, medical colleges, medical students
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to next — national exit test under the NMC Act.
scenarioTags: next — national exit test under NMC Act

title: Drug Technical Advisory Board — DTAB
definition: Section 9B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Drug Technical Advisory Board — DTAB".
simplifiedExplanation: DTAB advises central and state governments on technical matters related to drugs. Most important advisory body on drug policy. Comprises technical experts, pharmacologists, and officials.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to drug technical advisory board — dtab under the Drugs Act.
scenarioTags: drug technical advisory board — dtab under Drugs Act

title: Standards of Quality — Indian Pharmacopoeia
definition: Section 16 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Standards of Quality — Indian Pharmacopoeia".
simplifiedExplanation: Drugs must conform to standards in the Indian Pharmacopoeia. Drugs not conforming are considered 'not of standard quality'. The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission maintains these standards.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to standards of quality — indian pharmacopoeia under the Drugs Act.
scenarioTags: standards of quality — indian pharmacopoeia under Drugs Act

title: Misbranded Drugs
definition: Section 17 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Misbranded Drugs".
simplifiedExplanation: A drug is misbranded if: (1) label is false or misleading, (2) imitates another drug, (3) not labelled as prescribed, (4) expiry date is wrong. Selling misbranded drugs is punishable.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to misbranded drugs under the Drugs Act.

title: Adulterated Drugs
definition: Section 17A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Adulterated Drugs".
simplifiedExplanation: A drug is adulterated if its strength/quality/purity falls below prescribed standards, or if any substance has been mixed to reduce quality. Adulterated drugs can be dangerous to health.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to adulterated drugs under the Drugs Act.

title: Spurious Drugs
definition: Section 17B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Spurious Drugs".
simplifiedExplanation: A drug is spurious if: (1) it is manufactured under a false name, (2) it imitates another drug, (3) actual manufacturer's name is not stated, (4) it is substituted wholly or partly. Spurious drugs causing death: up to life imprisonment.
punishment: 10 years to life imprisonment if causing death + ₹10 lakh fine
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to spurious drugs under the Drugs Act.

title: Prohibition of Manufacture and Sale of Certain Drugs
definition: Section 18 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Prohibition of Manufacture and Sale of Certain Drugs".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall manufacture, sell, or distribute: (1) misbranded drugs, (2) adulterated drugs, (3) spurious drugs, (4) drugs without licence, (5) drugs not of standard quality. Drug Inspector can enter and inspect any premises.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs under the Drugs Act.
tags: prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs
aiSearchKeywords: prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs
scenarioTags: prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs under Drugs Act

title: Drug Licence Required
definition: Section 22 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Drug Licence Required".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall manufacture any drug without a licence granted by the State Licensing Authority. Different licences for manufacturing, selling, importing. Manufacturing must comply with Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP).
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to drug licence required under the Drugs Act.
scenarioTags: drug licence required under Drugs Act

title: Power to Prohibit Manufacture and Sale of Drug
definition: Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Power to Prohibit Manufacture and Sale of Drug".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can prohibit manufacture/sale of any drug that is likely to cause risk to health or has no therapeutic value. Used to ban drugs like Ranitidine (Zantac) and FDC drugs.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to prohibit manufacture and sale of drug under the Drugs Act.
tags: power to prohibit manufacture and sale of drug
aiSearchKeywords: power to prohibit manufacture and sale of drug
scenarioTags: power to prohibit manufacture and sale of drug under Drugs Act

title: Penalty for Contravention
definition: Section 27 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Penalty for Contravention".
simplifiedExplanation: Manufacturing, selling, distributing adulterated or spurious drugs is punishable with heavy penalties. Repeat offenders get enhanced punishment. Death caused by spurious drugs can attract life imprisonment.
punishment: First offence: 1-2 years + fine. Second offence: 2-4 years + fine. Spurious drugs: 10 years to life
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for contravention under the Drugs Act.
scenarioTags: penalty for contravention under Drugs Act

title: Drug Controller General of India — DCGI
definition: Section 33EEB of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 deals with "Drug Controller General of India — DCGI".
simplifiedExplanation: DCGI is the head of CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation). Approves new drugs, clinical trials, import of drugs. DCGI's approval is needed before any new drug can be marketed in India.
whoItAppliesTo: Drug manufacturers, importers, sellers, pharmacists
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to drug controller general of india — dcgi under the Drugs Act.

scenarioTags: drug controller general of india — dcgi under Drugs Act

title: When Pregnancy Can Be Terminated
definition: Section 3 of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "When Pregnancy Can Be Terminated".
simplifiedExplanation: After 2021 Amendment: (1) Up to 20 weeks: 1 doctor's opinion, (2) 20-24 weeks: 2 doctors' opinion — only for specific categories (rape survivors, minors, change of marital status, physical disability, foetal abnormality), (3) Any time: if Medical Board certifies substantial foetal abnormality.
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to when pregnancy can be terminated under the MTP Act.
scenarioTags: when pregnancy can be terminated under MTP Act

title: Grounds for MTP
definition: Section 3(2) of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "Grounds for MTP".
simplifiedExplanation: Pregnancy can be terminated if: (1) continuance would involve risk to life or physical/mental health of mother, (2) substantial risk of child being born with serious physical/mental abnormalities. FAILURE OF CONTRACEPTION is a valid ground for married AND unmarried women (after 2021 amendment).
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to grounds for mtp under the MTP Act.
scenarioTags: grounds for mtp under MTP Act

title: Specific Categories for 20-24 Weeks
definition: Section 3(2B) of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "Specific Categories for 20-24 Weeks".
simplifiedExplanation: Categories eligible for termination between 20-24 weeks: (a) survivors of sexual assault/rape, (b) minors, (c) change in marital status (divorce/widowhood) during pregnancy, (d) women with physical disabilities, (e) mentally ill women, (f) foetal malformation, (g) women in humanitarian/disaster situations.
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to specific categories for 20-24 weeks under the MTP Act.
scenarioTags: specific categories for 20-24 weeks under MTP Act

title: Place Where Pregnancy May Be Terminated
definition: Section 4 of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "Place Where Pregnancy May Be Terminated".
simplifiedExplanation: MTP can only be done at a government hospital or a place approved by the government. Private clinics must have government approval. This ensures safety standards.
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to place where pregnancy may be terminated under the MTP Act.
tags: place where pregnancy may be terminated
aiSearchKeywords: place where pregnancy may be terminated
scenarioTags: place where pregnancy may be terminated under MTP Act

title: Medical Board for Foetal Abnormalities
definition: Section 5 of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "Medical Board for Foetal Abnormalities".
simplifiedExplanation: For pregnancies beyond 24 weeks: a Medical Board (established by state government) must examine and certify substantial foetal abnormality. The Board makes the final decision. No time limit if Board certifies abnormality.
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to medical board for foetal abnormalities under the MTP Act.
scenarioTags: medical board for foetal abnormalities under MTP Act

title: Confidentiality
definition: Section 5A of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971 deals with "Confidentiality".
simplifiedExplanation: Name and details of the woman undergoing MTP cannot be revealed except to a person authorized by law. Breach of confidentiality: imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
whoItAppliesTo: Pregnant women, registered medical practitioners
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to confidentiality under the MTP Act.

lawName: Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994
title: Prohibition of Sex Selection
definition: Section 3A of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994 deals with "Prohibition of Sex Selection".
simplifiedExplanation: No person (including doctor or clinic) shall conduct or help in conducting pre-conception sex selection. Sex selection BEFORE and DURING pregnancy is completely banned in India.
whoItAppliesTo: Doctors, labs, clinics performing pre-natal diagnostic tests, pregnant women
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of sex selection under the PCPNDT Act.
scenarioTags: prohibition of sex selection under PCPNDT Act

lawName: Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994
title: Regulation of Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques
definition: Section 4 of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994 deals with "Regulation of Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques".
simplifiedExplanation: Pre-natal diagnostic techniques (ultrasound, amniocentesis) can ONLY be used to detect: (1) genetic abnormalities, (2) metabolic disorders, (3) chromosomal abnormalities, (4) sex-linked disorders. Conducting tests for sex determination is ILLEGAL.
whoItAppliesTo: Doctors, labs, clinics performing pre-natal diagnostic tests, pregnant women

simplifiedExplanation: No person conducting pre-natal test shall communicate the sex of the foetus to the pregnant woman or her relatives by words, signs, or in any other manner. Even hinting at the sex is illegal.
whoItAppliesTo: Doctors, labs, clinics performing pre-natal diagnostic tests, pregnant women

title: Determination of Sex Prohibited
definition: Section 6 of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994 deals with "Determination of Sex Prohibited".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall conduct or cause to be conducted pre-natal sex determination. Advertising sex determination services is also prohibited. Includes online/digital advertising.

title: Prohibition of Advertisement
definition: Section 22 of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act 1994 deals with "Prohibition of Advertisement".
simplifiedExplanation: No advertisement of any technique for sex determination or sex selection shall be published. Contravention: 3 years imprisonment + ₹10,000 fine. Print media, TV, online — all are covered.
whoItAppliesTo: Doctors, labs, clinics performing pre-natal diagnostic tests, pregnant women
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of advertisement under the PCPNDT Act.

simplifiedExplanation: Doctor conducting sex determination: imprisoned + name permanently removed from medical register. Clinic conducting tests: registration cancelled. Pregnant woman undergoing test: NOT punishable (she is presumed to have been compelled).
punishment: First offence: 3 years + ₹10,000 fine. Subsequent offence: 5 years + ₹50,000 fine. Name struck off medical register.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Right of Child to Free and Compulsory Education
definition: Section 3 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Right of Child to Free and Compulsory Education".
simplifiedExplanation: Every child aged 6-14 has the fundamental right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school. Free = no fee or charges. Compulsory = it is the government's duty to ensure admission, attendance, and completion of elementary education.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right of child to free and compulsory education under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Special Provision for Dropped-Out Children
definition: Section 4 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Special Provision for Dropped-Out Children".
simplifiedExplanation: A child above 6 who has not been admitted or dropped out shall be admitted in an age-appropriate class and given special training to be at par with other children.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to special provision for dropped-out children under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Right to Transfer to Other School
definition: Section 5 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Right to Transfer to Other School".
simplifiedExplanation: A child can transfer to any other school. If no transfer certificate is available, the headteacher must immediately admit the child and not delay admission.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to transfer to other school under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Duty of Government to Establish Schools
definition: Section 6 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Duty of Government to Establish Schools".
simplifiedExplanation: Government must establish schools within 1 km walking distance for classes 1-5, and within 3 km for classes 6-8. Where school is not possible, government must arrange for transport or residential facilities.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to duty of government to establish schools under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Duties of Central Government

simplifiedExplanation: Central Government must: (1) develop national curriculum framework, (2) develop and enforce standards for teacher training, (3) provide technical support to states.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to duties of central government under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: 25% Reservation for Economically Weaker Sections
definition: Section 12(1)(c) of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "25% Reservation for Economically Weaker Sections".
simplifiedExplanation: Every private unaided school must admit at least 25% of its seats from EWS/disadvantaged groups at entry-level classes. Government reimburses the school for fees. This is the most debated provision.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: No Capitation Fee or Screening
definition: Section 13 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "No Capitation Fee or Screening".
simplifiedExplanation: No school shall charge capitation fee. No child shall be subjected to any screening procedure for admission. Admission shall be through lottery if applications exceed available seats. Donation for admission is illegal.
punishment: Capitation fee: fine up to 10x the amount charged. Screening: fine up to ₹25,000, then ₹50,000
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to no capitation fee or screening under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Proof of Age for Admission
definition: Section 14 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Proof of Age for Admission".
simplifiedExplanation: No child can be denied admission for lack of age proof. Parents' declaration is sufficient. Birth certificate, hospital certificate, Anganwadi record, or even a self-declaration by parent is accepted.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to proof of age for admission under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: No Detention Policy
definition: Section 16 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "No Detention Policy".
simplifiedExplanation: No child shall be held back in any class or expelled until completion of elementary education (Class 8). This no-detention policy was amended in 2019 to allow states to hold back students in Class 5 and Class 8 if they fail exams.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to no detention policy under the RTE Act.
scenarioTags: no detention policy under RTE Act

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Prohibition of Physical Punishment
definition: Section 17 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Prohibition of Physical Punishment".
simplifiedExplanation: No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. Teacher who violates this is subject to disciplinary action. This includes corporal punishment, verbal abuse, and discrimination.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition of physical punishment under the RTE Act.
scenarioTags: prohibition of physical punishment under RTE Act

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Qualifications of Teachers
definition: Section 23 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Qualifications of Teachers".
simplifiedExplanation: Teachers must have minimum qualification as prescribed by academic authority (NCTE). All existing teachers who don't meet qualifications must acquire them within 5 years. Untrained teachers cannot be appointed.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to qualifications of teachers under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Pupil-Teacher Ratio
definition: Section 25 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Pupil-Teacher Ratio".
simplifiedExplanation: For primary school (1-5): 30 students per teacher. For upper primary (6-8): 35 students per teacher. Schools not meeting PTR must comply within 3 years.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to pupil-teacher ratio under the RTE Act.

lawName: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
title: Curriculum and Evaluation
definition: Section 29 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 deals with "Curriculum and Evaluation".
simplifiedExplanation: Academic authority must prescribe curriculum with focus on: all-round development, child's knowledge/potential/talent, activity-based learning, comprehensive and continuous evaluation, no board exam until Class 8.
whoItAppliesTo: All children aged 6-14 years, schools, state governments

title: Monitoring of Child's Right to Education

simplifiedExplanation: NCPCR (National Commission for Protection of Child Rights) and SCPCRs monitor and review implementation of RTE. They can examine complaints and take suo motu cognizance.

simplifiedExplanation: Any person having grievance about violation of RTE can file complaint to the local authority. If not resolved, can approach SCPCR or NCPCR. These commissions have powers of a civil court.

title: Establishment of UGC

title: Functions of UGC
definition: Section 5 of the University Grants Commission Act 1956 deals with "Functions of UGC".
simplifiedExplanation: UGC: (1) grants recognition to universities, (2) allocates funds, (3) prescribes minimum standards, (4) advises universities, (5) regulates fees, (6) frames regulations on teacher qualifications. Most important regulatory body for higher education.

title: Grants by UGC
definition: Section 12 of the University Grants Commission Act 1956 deals with "Grants by UGC".
simplifiedExplanation: UGC allocates grants to universities and colleges for: (1) construction, (2) equipment, (3) research, (4) fellowships, (5) faculty improvement, (6) sports. Only UGC-recognized institutions get grants.

title: Right to Confer Degrees

title: Prohibition of Fake Degrees
definition: Section 23 of the University Grants Commission Act 1956 deals with "Prohibition of Fake Degrees".
simplifiedExplanation: Granting degrees without being a recognized university is punishable. UGC maintains a list of fake universities. Using a degree from a fake university is also punishable.

title: Power to Set Minimum Standards
definition: Section 26 of the University Grants Commission Act 1956 deals with "Power to Set Minimum Standards".
simplifiedExplanation: UGC can set minimum standards for: (1) courses, (2) examination, (3) research, (4) teacher qualifications, (5) library and laboratory facilities. Universities must comply.

realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to set minimum standards under the UGC Act.

title: Persons Subject to the Act
definition: Section 3 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Persons Subject to the Act".
simplifiedExplanation: The Act applies to: all officers, JCOs, warrant officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers of the Regular Army. Also applies to persons attached to or employed with the Army during operations.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to persons subject to the act under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: persons subject to the act under Army Act

title: Offences in Relation to the Enemy
definition: Section 34 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Offences in Relation to the Enemy".
simplifiedExplanation: Shamefully abandoning post, not engaging enemy, treacherously communicating with enemy, assisting the enemy, or showing cowardice — all punishable with death or life imprisonment. Most serious military offences.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offences in relation to the enemy under the Army Act.

title: Mutiny
definition: Section 37 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Mutiny".
simplifiedExplanation: Mutiny = joining in, or conspiring for, or not suppressing a mutiny. Any person who begins or conspires to cause mutiny is punishable with death. This is the most serious collective military offence.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to mutiny under the Army Act.

title: Desertion
definition: Section 38 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Desertion".
simplifiedExplanation: Leaving or failing to join the service without authority and with intention of not returning is desertion. On active service, desertion is punishable with death. In peacetime: up to 7 years imprisonment.
punishment: Up to 7 years imprisonment (active service: death)
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to desertion under the Army Act.

title: Absence Without Leave (AWOL)
definition: Section 39 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Absence Without Leave (AWOL)".
simplifiedExplanation: Absenting from duty without leave or overstaying leave is AWOL. Less serious than desertion because there's no intention of permanent absence. But repeated AWOL can lead to court martial.
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to absence without leave (awol) under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: absence without leave (awol) under Army Act

title: Striking or Threatening Superior Officer
definition: Section 40 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Striking or Threatening Superior Officer".
simplifiedExplanation: Using criminal force against or threatening a superior officer is a serious military offence. On active service, it is punishable with death. Discipline and chain of command are absolute in the military.
punishment: Up to 14 years imprisonment (active service: death)
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to striking or threatening superior officer under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: striking or threatening superior officer under Army Act

title: Disobedience to Superior Officer
definition: Section 41 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Disobedience to Superior Officer".
simplifiedExplanation: Disobeying a lawful command of a superior officer is a military offence. However, an unlawful order (like one violating human rights) need not be obeyed.
punishment: Up to 14 years imprisonment (active service: death)
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disobedience to superior officer under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: disobedience to superior officer under Army Act

title: Criminal Offences
definition: Section 52 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Criminal Offences".
simplifiedExplanation: Any offence under IPC/BNS committed by a person subject to the Army Act can be tried by court martial. So murder, theft, assault etc. can all be tried by military courts.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to criminal offences under the Army Act.

title: Civil Offences Tried by Court Martial
definition: Section 69 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Civil Offences Tried by Court Martial".
simplifiedExplanation: A court martial can try any person subject to Army Act for ANY offence under civilian criminal law. The choice between court martial and civil court depends on command decision.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to civil offences tried by court martial under the Army Act.

title: General Court Martial — Composition
definition: Section 108 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "General Court Martial — Composition".
simplifiedExplanation: General Court Martial (GCM): minimum 5 officers, presided by an officer of Colonel rank or above. Can try any offence and award any punishment including death. Most serious court martial.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to general court martial — composition under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: general court martial — composition under Army Act

title: District Court Martial
definition: Section 109 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "District Court Martial".
simplifiedExplanation: District Court Martial (DCM): minimum 3 officers. Cannot try officers above Captain rank. Cannot award death penalty, life imprisonment, or dismissal of officers. For lesser offences.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to district court martial under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: district court martial under Army Act

title: Summary Court Martial
definition: Section 110 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Summary Court Martial".
simplifiedExplanation: Summary Court Martial (SCM): held by a Commanding Officer. For quick disposal of minor offences on active service. Can award up to 1 year imprisonment for soldiers (not officers).
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to summary court martial under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: summary court martial under Army Act

title: Confirmation of Court Martial Sentences
definition: Section 125 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Confirmation of Court Martial Sentences".
simplifiedExplanation: All court martial sentences must be confirmed by the confirming authority (usually the area commander or higher). Death sentence requires confirmation by Central Government. Unconfirmed sentence is not valid.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to confirmation of court martial sentences under the Army Act.
scenarioTags: confirmation of court martial sentences under Army Act

title: Remedy Against Court Martial — Post-Confirmation Petition
definition: Section 164 of the Army Act 1950 deals with "Remedy Against Court Martial — Post-Confirmation Petition".
simplifiedExplanation: After confirmation, the convicted person can file a post-confirmation petition. If dismissed, can appeal to Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) and then to Supreme Court.
punishment: Court martial punishment up to death for serious offences
whoItAppliesTo: All persons subject to the Army Act — officers, JCOs, other ranks, and attached persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to remedy against court martial — post-confirmation petition under the Army Act.

scenarioTags: remedy against court martial — post-confirmation petition under Army Act

title: Declaration of Disturbed Area
definition: Section 3 of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958 deals with "Declaration of Disturbed Area".
simplifiedExplanation: Central or State Government can declare any area as 'disturbed area' if it is in such a disturbed condition that the use of armed forces is necessary. Once declared, AFSPA applies to that area. Currently applicable in parts of Manipur, Nagaland, Assam, J&K.
whoItAppliesTo: Armed forces operating in declared 'disturbed areas'
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to declaration of disturbed area under the AFSPA.
scenarioTags: declaration of disturbed area under AFSPA

title: Power to Fire — Even to Causing Death
definition: Section 4(a) of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958 deals with "Power to Fire — Even to Causing Death".
simplifiedExplanation: In a disturbed area, an officer can fire upon or use force — even to the extent of causing death — against any person acting in contravention of prohibitory orders. This is the most controversial provision.
whoItAppliesTo: Armed forces operating in declared 'disturbed areas'
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to fire — even to causing death under the AFSPA.

title: Power to Arrest Without Warrant
definition: Section 4(c) of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958 deals with "Power to Arrest Without Warrant".
simplifiedExplanation: Armed forces can arrest without warrant any person who has committed or is about to commit a cognizable offence. Arrested person must be handed over to nearest police station with minimum delay.
whoItAppliesTo: Armed forces operating in declared 'disturbed areas'
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to arrest without warrant under the AFSPA.

title: Power to Enter and Search Without Warrant
definition: Section 4(d) of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958 deals with "Power to Enter and Search Without Warrant".
simplifiedExplanation: Armed forces can enter and search any premises without warrant to make arrests or recover property/arms. This overrides normal legal protections against unreasonable search.
whoItAppliesTo: Armed forces operating in declared 'disturbed areas'
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to enter and search without warrant under the AFSPA.

title: Protection of Persons Acting Under AFSPA
definition: Section 6 of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958 deals with "Protection of Persons Acting Under AFSPA".
simplifiedExplanation: No prosecution or legal proceeding can be started against any armed forces personnel acting under AFSPA without prior sanction of the Central Government. This creates near-total immunity.
whoItAppliesTo: Armed forces operating in declared 'disturbed areas'
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to protection of persons acting under afspa under the AFSPA.

title: Power to Make Orders Detaining Certain Persons
definition: Section 3 of the National Security Act 1980 deals with "Power to Make Orders Detaining Certain Persons".
simplifiedExplanation: Central or State Government or DM can detain any person if satisfied it is necessary to prevent them from acting in a manner prejudicial to: (1) defence of India, (2) security of India, (3) security of state, (4) maintenance of public order, (5) maintenance of essential supplies.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who can be detained to prevent acts prejudicial to national security or public order
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to make orders detaining certain persons under the NSA.
