scenarioTags: power to make orders detaining certain persons under NSA

title: Communication of Grounds of Detention
definition: Section 5A of the National Security Act 1980 deals with "Communication of Grounds of Detention".
simplifiedExplanation: The detaining authority must communicate the grounds of detention to the detainee within 5 days (exceptionally 10 days). Grounds must be in a language the detainee understands. Failure = detention is void.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who can be detained to prevent acts prejudicial to national security or public order
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to communication of grounds of detention under the NSA.
scenarioTags: communication of grounds of detention under NSA

title: Advisory Board
definition: Section 8 of the National Security Act 1980 deals with "Advisory Board".
simplifiedExplanation: Government must place the detention order before an Advisory Board within 3 weeks. Board must report within 7 weeks. Board comprises High Court judges. If Board says detention is not justified — person must be released.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who can be detained to prevent acts prejudicial to national security or public order
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to advisory board under the NSA.

title: Revocation of Detention Order
definition: Section 10 of the National Security Act 1980 deals with "Revocation of Detention Order".
simplifiedExplanation: Government can revoke a detention order at any time. But revocation doesn't prevent fresh detention on same or different grounds.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who can be detained to prevent acts prejudicial to national security or public order
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to revocation of detention order under the NSA.
scenarioTags: revocation of detention order under NSA

title: Maximum Period of Detention
definition: Section 13 of the National Security Act 1980 deals with "Maximum Period of Detention".
simplifiedExplanation: Maximum detention period: 12 months. Can be extended only with Advisory Board approval. After 12 months, fresh order needed with fresh grounds. Detention without trial for up to 1 year is the most criticized aspect.
whoItAppliesTo: Any person who can be detained to prevent acts prejudicial to national security or public order
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to maximum period of detention under the NSA.
scenarioTags: maximum period of detention under NSA

title: Penalties for Spying
definition: Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act 1923 deals with "Penalties for Spying".
simplifiedExplanation: Approaching, inspecting, passing over a prohibited place, obtaining secret information, communicating it to a foreign power or enemy — all punishable. This is the anti-espionage provision.
whoItAppliesTo: Government employees, spies, journalists, anyone handling classified information
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalties for spying under the OSA.

title: Wrongful Communication of Information
definition: Section 5 of the Official Secrets Act 1923 deals with "Wrongful Communication of Information".
simplifiedExplanation: Any government servant who communicates official secrets to unauthorized persons. Also covers journalists who receive and publish classified information. Very broad — even embarrassing (not security-related) information is covered.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment (up to 14 years for sensitive information)
whoItAppliesTo: Government employees, spies, journalists, anyone handling classified information
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to wrongful communication of information under the OSA.
scenarioTags: wrongful communication of information under OSA

title: Unauthorized Use of Uniforms and Falsification of Reports
definition: Section 6 of the Official Secrets Act 1923 deals with "Unauthorized Use of Uniforms and Falsification of Reports".
simplifiedExplanation: Wearing military/police uniform without authority, or making false reports, to gain access to prohibited places is punishable.
whoItAppliesTo: Government employees, spies, journalists, anyone handling classified information
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to unauthorized use of uniforms and falsification of reports under the OSA.
tags: unauthorized use of uniforms and falsification of reports
aiSearchKeywords: unauthorized use of uniforms and falsification of reports
scenarioTags: unauthorized use of uniforms and falsification of reports under OSA

title: Penalty for Harbouring Spies
definition: Section 10 of the Official Secrets Act 1923 deals with "Penalty for Harbouring Spies".
simplifiedExplanation: Harbouring or concealing a person who has committed an offence under this Act is itself a crime.
whoItAppliesTo: Government employees, spies, journalists, anyone handling classified information
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for harbouring spies under the OSA.
scenarioTags: penalty for harbouring spies under OSA

title: National Electricity Policy and Plan
definition: Section 3 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "National Electricity Policy and Plan".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government formulates National Electricity Policy and Tariff Policy. Objective: supply electricity to all areas including villages, at affordable prices, with competition and efficiency.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to national electricity policy and plan under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: national electricity policy and plan under Electricity Act

title: Generating Company — No Licence Required
definition: Section 7 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Generating Company — No Licence Required".
simplifiedExplanation: Any generating company can establish, operate, and maintain a generating station without obtaining a licence. Only techno-economic clearance needed for hydro projects. This opened up electricity generation to private sector.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to generating company — no licence required under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: generating company — no licence required under Electricity Act

title: Licence for Transmission and Distribution
definition: Section 14 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Licence for Transmission and Distribution".
simplifiedExplanation: No person can transmit or supply electricity in an area without a licence from the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. Licence is area-specific and time-bound (25 years, renewable).
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to licence for transmission and distribution under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: licence for transmission and distribution under Electricity Act

title: Open Access to Distribution System
definition: Section 42 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Open Access to Distribution System".
simplifiedExplanation: Open access allows any consumer with load above 1 MW to buy electricity from any generator — not just the local distribution company. This introduces competition. Surcharge and cross-subsidy surcharge apply.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to open access to distribution system under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: open access to distribution system under Electricity Act

title: Duty to Supply Electricity
definition: Section 43 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Duty to Supply Electricity".
simplifiedExplanation: Every distribution licensee must supply electricity to any person (owner/occupier) within the licensed area on application. Cannot refuse supply to any class of consumers. Supply must be within 1 month of application.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to duty to supply electricity under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: duty to supply electricity under Electricity Act

title: Disconnection of Supply for Non-Payment
definition: Section 56 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Disconnection of Supply for Non-Payment".
simplifiedExplanation: Distribution company can disconnect supply if consumer doesn't pay bills after 15-day notice. But cannot disconnect during: medical emergency (if oxygen concentrator etc. is running), pending dispute before consumer grievance forum.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to disconnection of supply for non-payment under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: disconnection of supply for non-payment under Electricity Act

title: Tariff Determination by Regulatory Commission
definition: Section 62 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Tariff Determination by Regulatory Commission".
simplifiedExplanation: Electricity tariff is determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC). SERC holds public hearings before fixing tariffs. Tariff must be cost-reflective but affordable.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to tariff determination by regulatory commission under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: tariff determination by regulatory commission under Electricity Act

title: Central Electricity Regulatory Commission — CERC
definition: Section 79 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Central Electricity Regulatory Commission — CERC".
simplifiedExplanation: CERC regulates: (1) inter-state transmission tariffs, (2) inter-state generation tariffs, (3) grants licences for inter-state transmission. CERC also regulates power exchanges.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to central electricity regulatory commission — cerc under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: central electricity regulatory commission — cerc under Electricity Act

title: State Electricity Regulatory Commission — SERC
definition: Section 86 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "State Electricity Regulatory Commission — SERC".
simplifiedExplanation: SERC regulates: (1) intra-state tariffs, (2) grants distribution licences, (3) promotes competition, (4) advises state government on electricity policy. Each state has its own SERC.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to state electricity regulatory commission — serc under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: state electricity regulatory commission — serc under Electricity Act

title: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity — APTEL
definition: Section 111 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Appellate Tribunal for Electricity — APTEL".
simplifiedExplanation: APTEL hears appeals against orders of CERC, SERC, and adjudicating officers. Located in New Delhi. Further appeal lies to Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to appellate tribunal for electricity — aptel under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: appellate tribunal for electricity — aptel under Electricity Act

title: Unauthorized Use of Electricity — Assessment
definition: Section 126 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Unauthorized Use of Electricity — Assessment".
simplifiedExplanation: If electricity is used by tampering with meter, bypassing meter, or other unauthorized means, the licensee can assess the quantum of electricity consumed and charge at 1.5x the normal tariff for the assessed period.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to unauthorized use of electricity — assessment under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: unauthorized use of electricity — assessment under Electricity Act

title: Theft of Electricity
definition: Section 135 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Theft of Electricity".
simplifiedExplanation: Theft of electricity includes: meter tampering, using hook/loop connection, bypassing meter, unauthorized reconnection. Electricity theft is a cognizable and non-bailable offence.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine (up to 5 years for subsequent offence)
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to theft of electricity under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: theft of electricity under Electricity Act

title: Interference with Meters
definition: Section 138 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Interference with Meters".
simplifiedExplanation: Tampering with, destroying, or interfering with electricity meters is a criminal offence. Also covers unauthorized connection to distribution lines.
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to interference with meters under the Electricity Act.
scenarioTags: interference with meters under Electricity Act

title: Penalty for Non-Compliance with ERC Orders
definition: Section 152 of the Electricity Act 2003 deals with "Penalty for Non-Compliance with ERC Orders".
simplifiedExplanation: Non-compliance with orders of CERC, SERC, or APTEL is punishable with fine. Continued non-compliance attracts daily penalty.
punishment: Up to ₹1 lakh + additional ₹6,000 per day of continued non-compliance
whoItAppliesTo: Electricity generation, transmission, distribution companies, consumers
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for non-compliance with erc orders under the Electricity Act.
tags: penalty for non-compliance with erc orders
aiSearchKeywords: penalty for non-compliance with erc orders
scenarioTags: penalty for non-compliance with erc orders under Electricity Act

title: Authorization for Telecom Services
definition: Section 3 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "Authorization for Telecom Services".
simplifiedExplanation: No person can establish, operate, or maintain a telecommunications network or provide telecom services without an authorization from the Central Government. This replaces the old licensing regime.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to authorization for telecom services under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: authorization for telecom services under Telecom Act

title: Spectrum Assignment
definition: Section 4 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "Spectrum Assignment".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government assigns spectrum through: (1) auction, (2) administrative process for government use, satellite, backhaul etc. Spectrum is a natural resource belonging to the people. Assignment is for a specific period (20 years typically).
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to spectrum assignment under the Telecom Act.

title: Right of Way
definition: Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "Right of Way".
simplifiedExplanation: Telecom entities have the right to establish infrastructure (towers, cables, ducts) in public property. Local authorities must facilitate. Cannot unreasonably delay or deny permissions.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right of way under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: right of way under Telecom Act

title: Interception and Monitoring
definition: Section 24 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "Interception and Monitoring".
simplifiedExplanation: Central or State Government can direct interception/monitoring of telecom messages in the interest of sovereignty, security, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, or preventing incitement to offence. Must be authorized by Secretary-level officer.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to interception and monitoring under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: interception and monitoring under Telecom Act

title: Internet Shutdown Powers
definition: Section 25 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "Internet Shutdown Powers".
simplifiedExplanation: Government can suspend telecom services (internet shutdown) in case of public emergency or public safety. Must be reviewed by a Review Committee within 5 working days. Has been widely criticized by civil society.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to internet shutdown powers under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: internet shutdown powers under Telecom Act

title: TRAI — Regulatory Functions
definition: Section 46 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "TRAI — Regulatory Functions".
simplifiedExplanation: TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India) regulates tariffs, interconnection, quality of service, and consumer protection in telecom. TRAI is only recommendatory — final decisions are taken by the government.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to trai — regulatory functions under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: trai — regulatory functions under Telecom Act

title: TDSAT — Telecom Disputes Settlement
definition: Section 48 of the Telecommunications Act 2023 deals with "TDSAT — Telecom Disputes Settlement".
simplifiedExplanation: TDSAT (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal) adjudicates disputes between licensees, and appeals against TRAI orders. Further appeal to Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: Telecom companies, internet service providers, users
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to tdsat — telecom disputes settlement under the Telecom Act.
scenarioTags: tdsat — telecom disputes settlement under Telecom Act

title: Central Government Control of Atomic Energy
definition: Section 3 of the Atomic Energy Act 1962 deals with "Central Government Control of Atomic Energy".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government has exclusive control over all aspects of atomic energy: production, development, use, and disposal of atomic energy and nuclear substances. No private entity can deal in nuclear materials without government permission.
whoItAppliesTo: Government of India, DAE, BARC, NPCIL, all persons dealing with nuclear materials
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to central government control of atomic energy under the Atomic Energy Act.
tags: central government control of atomic energy
aiSearchKeywords: central government control of atomic energy
scenarioTags: central government control of atomic energy under Atomic Energy Act

title: Restrictions on Disclosure of Information
definition: Section 14 of the Atomic Energy Act 1962 deals with "Restrictions on Disclosure of Information".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall communicate to any unauthorized person any restricted information about atomic energy. This is the nuclear secrecy provision — stricter than Official Secrets Act.
whoItAppliesTo: Government of India, DAE, BARC, NPCIL, all persons dealing with nuclear materials
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to restrictions on disclosure of information under the Atomic Energy Act.
scenarioTags: restrictions on disclosure of information under Atomic Energy Act

title: Offences and Penalties
definition: Section 18 of the Atomic Energy Act 1962 deals with "Offences and Penalties".
simplifiedExplanation: Unauthorized possession, use, transfer, export of nuclear materials is punishable. Penalty can go up to life imprisonment for offences endangering national security.
punishment: Up to 5 years imprisonment + fine (up to life imprisonment for serious cases)
whoItAppliesTo: Government of India, DAE, BARC, NPCIL, all persons dealing with nuclear materials
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offences and penalties under the Atomic Energy Act.
scenarioTags: offences and penalties under Atomic Energy Act

title: Power of Central Government to Make Rules
definition: Section 20 of the Atomic Energy Act 1962 deals with "Power of Central Government to Make Rules".
simplifiedExplanation: Government can make rules for: safety standards, disposal of radioactive waste, protection of workers from radiation, control of nuclear materials. AERB (Atomic Energy Regulatory Board) enforces these rules.
whoItAppliesTo: Government of India, DAE, BARC, NPCIL, all persons dealing with nuclear materials
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power of central government to make rules under the Atomic Energy Act.
tags: power of central government to make rules
aiSearchKeywords: power of central government to make rules
scenarioTags: power of central government to make rules under Atomic Energy Act

title: Notice of Opening and Reopening of Mines
definition: Section 12 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Notice of Opening and Reopening of Mines".
simplifiedExplanation: Notice must be given to Chief Inspector at least 30 days before opening a new mine or reopening a closed one. Must include mine plan, safety plan, and ventilation scheme.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to notice of opening and reopening of mines under the Mines Act.
tags: notice of opening and reopening of mines
aiSearchKeywords: notice of opening and reopening of mines
scenarioTags: notice of opening and reopening of mines under Mines Act

title: Appointment of Manager
definition: Section 16 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Appointment of Manager".
simplifiedExplanation: Every mine must have a qualified manager who is responsible for control, management, and supervision of the mine. Manager must hold a Manager's Certificate.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to appointment of manager under the Mines Act.
scenarioTags: appointment of manager under Mines Act

title: Working Hours
definition: Section 18 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Working Hours".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall work in a mine for more than 48 hours per week or 9 hours per day. Rest day: 1 day per week. Night shift (7 PM to 6 AM): special restrictions apply for women workers.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to working hours under the Mines Act.

title: Weekly Day of Rest
definition: Section 19 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Weekly Day of Rest".
simplifiedExplanation: Every worker must get at least 1 day of rest per week. If required to work on rest day, compensatory rest day must be given within the same month.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to weekly day of rest under the Mines Act.
scenarioTags: weekly day of rest under Mines Act

title: Employment of Women and Children
definition: Section 22 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Employment of Women and Children".
simplifiedExplanation: No child below 18 shall be employed in a mine. Women can work in mines but not underground (above ground operations only). Working hours restrictions apply.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to employment of women and children under the Mines Act.
scenarioTags: employment of women and children under Mines Act

title: Safety Provisions
definition: Section 23 of the Mines Act 1952 deals with "Safety Provisions".
simplifiedExplanation: Mine owner must ensure: proper ventilation, drainage, prevention of fire and flood, safe means of entry/exit, adequate lighting, safe storage of explosives, and dust suppression.
whoItAppliesTo: Mine owners, managers, workers in all mines
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to safety provisions under the Mines Act.

title: Constitution of Panchayats
definition: Article 243B of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Constitution of Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: Every state shall constitute Panchayats at village, intermediate, and district levels. Three-tier system: (1) Gram Panchayat (village), (2) Panchayat Samiti (block/intermediate), (3) Zilla Parishad (district). States with population under 20 lakh may skip intermediate level.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to constitution of panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.

title: Composition of Panchayats
definition: Article 243C of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Composition of Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: Members of Panchayats are directly elected by the people. Chairperson of intermediate and district level may be elected directly or indirectly as per state law.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to composition of panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.

title: Reservation of Seats
definition: Article 243D of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Reservation of Seats".
simplifiedExplanation: Seats reserved for: (1) SC/ST in proportion to their population, (2) not less than 1/3 of total seats reserved for women (including SC/ST women). Offices of chairpersons also reserved for SC/ST/women. This is the most progressive reservation provision.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to reservation of seats under the 73rd Amendment.

title: Duration of Panchayats
definition: Article 243E of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Duration of Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: Every Panchayat shall continue for 5 years from its first meeting. Elections must be completed BEFORE the expiry of 5 years. If dissolved earlier, election within 6 months. Cannot be extended by state.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to duration of panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.

title: Powers and Functions of Panchayats
definition: Article 243G of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Powers and Functions of Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: State may endow Panchayats with powers to prepare plans for economic development and social justice. Includes subjects listed in 11th Schedule (29 subjects): agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, fisheries, education, health, rural housing, drinking water, roads, poverty alleviation.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to powers and functions of panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.
scenarioTags: powers and functions of panchayats under 73rd Amendment

title: Powers to Impose Taxes by Panchayats
definition: Article 243H of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "Powers to Impose Taxes by Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: State may authorize Panchayats to levy, collect, and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, and fees. This gives them independent revenue sources — not just dependence on state grants.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to powers to impose taxes by panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.
tags: powers to impose taxes by panchayats
aiSearchKeywords: powers to impose taxes by panchayats
scenarioTags: powers to impose taxes by panchayats under 73rd Amendment

title: State Finance Commission
definition: Article 243I of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "State Finance Commission".
simplifiedExplanation: Governor must constitute a Finance Commission every 5 years to review finances of Panchayats and recommend: distribution of taxes between state and Panchayats, grants-in-aid, measures to improve financial position.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to state finance commission under the 73rd Amendment.

title: State Election Commission
definition: Article 243K of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "State Election Commission".
simplifiedExplanation: State Election Commission (not Election Commission of India) conducts Panchayat elections. Headed by State Election Commissioner appointed by Governor. SEC is independent of state government.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to state election commission under the 73rd Amendment.

title: District Planning Committee
definition: Article 243ZD of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "District Planning Committee".
simplifiedExplanation: Every state must constitute a District Planning Committee to consolidate plans prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities in the district. DPC prepares a development plan for the entire district.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to district planning committee under the 73rd Amendment.

title: 29 Subjects for Panchayats
definition: 11th Schedule of the Constitution of India — Part IX (Panchayats) deals with "29 Subjects for Panchayats".
simplifiedExplanation: 11th Schedule lists 29 subjects that Panchayats may handle: 1. Agriculture, 2. Land improvement, 3. Minor irrigation, 4. Animal husbandry, 5. Fisheries, 6. Social forestry, 7. Minor forest produce, 8. Small scale industries, 9. Khadi/village industries, 10. Rural housing... and 19 more.
whoItAppliesTo: All three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to 29 subjects for panchayats under the 73rd Amendment.

title: Constitution of Municipalities
definition: Article 243Q of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "Constitution of Municipalities".
simplifiedExplanation: Three types of municipalities: (1) Nagar Panchayat — transitional area (rural to urban), (2) Municipal Council — smaller urban area, (3) Municipal Corporation — larger urban area. All are constituted by state law.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to constitution of municipalities under the 74th Amendment.

title: Composition of Municipalities
definition: Article 243R of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "Composition of Municipalities".
simplifiedExplanation: Members directly elected. Chairperson elected as per state law. Persons with special knowledge (without voting rights) can be nominated. MPs and MLAs of the area are members.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to composition of municipalities under the 74th Amendment.

title: Reservation of Seats in Municipalities
definition: Article 243T of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "Reservation of Seats in Municipalities".
simplifiedExplanation: Same as Panchayats: seats reserved for SC/ST in proportion to population. Not less than 1/3 seats reserved for women. Chairperson posts also reserved. OBC reservation as per state law.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to reservation of seats in municipalities under the 74th Amendment.
scenarioTags: reservation of seats in municipalities under 74th Amendment

title: Powers and Functions of Municipalities — 12th Schedule
definition: Article 243W of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "Powers and Functions of Municipalities — 12th Schedule".
simplifiedExplanation: 18 subjects in 12th Schedule: urban planning, land use regulation, roads, water supply, public health, fire services, urban forestry, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, street lighting, parking, etc.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to powers and functions of municipalities — 12th schedule under the 74th Amendment.
tags: powers and functions of municipalities — 12th schedule
aiSearchKeywords: powers and functions of municipalities — 12th schedule
scenarioTags: powers and functions of municipalities — 12th schedule under 74th Amendment

title: Power to Impose Taxes by Municipalities
definition: Article 243X of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "Power to Impose Taxes by Municipalities".
simplifiedExplanation: State may authorize municipalities to levy property tax, profession tax, entertainment tax, advertisement tax, and other local taxes. Property tax is the primary source of municipal revenue.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to impose taxes by municipalities under the 74th Amendment.
tags: power to impose taxes by municipalities
aiSearchKeywords: power to impose taxes by municipalities
scenarioTags: power to impose taxes by municipalities under 74th Amendment

title: State Finance Commission for Municipalities
definition: Article 243Y of the Constitution of India — Part IXA (Municipalities) deals with "State Finance Commission for Municipalities".
simplifiedExplanation: Same Finance Commission that reviews Panchayat finances also reviews municipal finances. Recommends grants-in-aid and measures to strengthen municipal financial position.
whoItAppliesTo: All urban local bodies — Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to state finance commission for municipalities under the 74th Amendment.
scenarioTags: state finance commission for municipalities under 74th Amendment

title: Supreme Court of India
definition: Article 124-147 of the Indian Court System deals with "Supreme Court of India".
simplifiedExplanation: Supreme Court is the apex court. 1 CJI + 33 judges (total 34). Sits in New Delhi. Has original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction. Under Article 141, law declared by Supreme Court is binding on ALL courts in India. Article 142: complete justice power.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to supreme court of india under the Courts.
scenarioTags: supreme court of india under Courts

title: High Courts
definition: Article 214-232 of the Indian Court System deals with "High Courts".
simplifiedExplanation: 25 High Courts in India. Each state has one (some shared). HC has original jurisdiction in writ matters (Article 226), appellate jurisdiction over district courts, and supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts. HC can issue ALL 5 writs (wider scope than SC).
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to high courts under the Courts.

title: District Courts and Subordinate Courts
definition: Article 233-237 of the Indian Court System deals with "District Courts and Subordinate Courts".
simplifiedExplanation: District Court is the principal court at district level. Headed by District Judge appointed by Governor in consultation with HC. Below it: Civil Judge (Senior/Junior Division), Chief Judicial Magistrate, Judicial Magistrate. These handle 90% of cases in India.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to district courts and subordinate courts under the Courts.
scenarioTags: district courts and subordinate courts under Courts

title: Court Martial (Military Courts)
definition: Court Martial of the Indian Court System deals with "Court Martial (Military Courts)".
simplifiedExplanation: Three types: General Court Martial (5+ officers, any punishment), District Court Martial (3+ officers, limited punishment), Summary Court Martial (single officer, minor offences). Appeals go to Armed Forces Tribunal, then Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to court martial (military courts) under the Courts.

title: Family Courts
definition: Family Courts Act 1984 of the Indian Court System deals with "Family Courts".
simplifiedExplanation: Established for speedy settlement of family disputes: divorce, maintenance, custody, property disputes between spouses. Simplified procedure, no lawyers required (but allowed). Every city with 1 million+ population must have Family Courts.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to family courts under the Courts.

title: Consumer Dispute Redressal Commissions
definition: Consumer Courts of the Indian Court System deals with "Consumer Dispute Redressal Commissions".
simplifiedExplanation: Three tiers: District Commission (up to ₹1 crore), State Commission (₹1-10 crore), National Commission (₹10 crore+). Fast, cheap, no lawyer needed. Can file online. Complaint must be filed within 2 years.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to consumer dispute redressal commissions under the Courts.
scenarioTags: consumer dispute redressal commissions under Courts

title: National Green Tribunal (NGT)
definition: National Green Tribunal of the Indian Court System deals with "National Green Tribunal (NGT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Established under NGT Act 2010. Handles environmental disputes. Has power of civil court. Chairperson must be retired SC/HC judge. Five benches across India: Delhi (principal), Pune, Bhopal, Chennai, Kolkata.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to national green tribunal (ngt) under the Courts.

title: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)
definition: NCLT of the Indian Court System deals with "National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Handles: company disputes, insolvency/bankruptcy proceedings under IBC 2016, mergers/amalgamations, oppression and mismanagement. Appeals to NCLAT (Appellate Tribunal), then Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to national company law tribunal (nclt) under the Courts.
scenarioTags: national company law tribunal (nclt) under Courts

title: Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)
definition: DRT of the Indian Court System deals with "Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Banks and financial institutions file cases for recovery of debts above ₹20 lakh. Established under Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and FIs Act 1993. Appeals to DRAT (Appellate Tribunal).
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to debt recovery tribunal (drt) under the Courts.

title: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
definition: ITAT of the Indian Court System deals with "Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Second appellate authority for income tax disputes. Appeal from Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) comes to ITAT. ITAT is the final fact-finding authority. Further appeal to HC only on questions of law.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to income tax appellate tribunal (itat) under the Courts.
scenarioTags: income tax appellate tribunal (itat) under Courts

title: Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
definition: CAT of the Indian Court System deals with "Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Handles disputes of central government employees regarding recruitment, service conditions, promotion, pension. Established under Article 323A. 17 regular benches + circuit benches. Further appeal to HC.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to central administrative tribunal (cat) under the Courts.

title: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)
definition: SAT of the Indian Court System deals with "Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Hears appeals against orders of SEBI, Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), and Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI). Appeals to Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to securities appellate tribunal (sat) under the Courts.

title: Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT)
definition: AFT of the Indian Court System deals with "Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT)".
simplifiedExplanation: Handles: service matters and court martial appeals of armed forces personnel. Replaces HC jurisdiction in armed forces matters. Principal bench in New Delhi + regional benches. Further appeal to SC.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to armed forces tribunal (aft) under the Courts.

title: Lok Adalat (People's Court)
definition: Lok Adalat of the Indian Court System deals with "Lok Adalat (People's Court)".
simplifiedExplanation: Lok Adalat provides alternative dispute resolution. Award is binding and final — no appeal. No court fee. Covers: motor accident claims, matrimonial disputes, labour disputes, electricity disputes, dishonoured cheques. Cases can be referred by courts or filed directly.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to lok adalat (people's court) under the Courts.

title: Fast Track Courts and Special Courts
definition: Fast Track Courts of the Indian Court System deals with "Fast Track Courts and Special Courts".
simplifiedExplanation: Fast Track Courts for: rape cases (complete trial in 2 months), cases against MPs/MLAs, POCSO cases. Special Courts for: NIA (terrorism), CBI (corruption), PMLA (money laundering), SC/ST atrocities.
whoItAppliesTo: All litigants and legal professionals
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to fast track courts and special courts under the Courts.

title: Bar Council of India — Establishment
definition: Section 4 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Bar Council of India — Establishment".
simplifiedExplanation: Bar Council of India (BCI) is the apex body regulating the legal profession in India. It sets standards for legal education, professional conduct, and disciplinary matters. Located in New Delhi.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to bar council of india — establishment under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: bar council of india — establishment under Advocates Act

title: Functions of Bar Council of India
definition: Section 6 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Functions of Bar Council of India".
simplifiedExplanation: BCI: (1) sets standards of professional conduct, (2) safeguards rights of advocates, (3) promotes legal education, (4) recognizes universities for law degrees, (5) maintains All-India Bar Register, (6) disciplinary authority over advocates.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils

title: Functions of State Bar Council
definition: Section 7 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Functions of State Bar Council".
simplifiedExplanation: State Bar Councils: (1) admit persons as advocates, (2) maintain state roll of advocates, (3) entertain complaints against advocates, (4) conduct disciplinary proceedings. Each state has its own State Bar Council.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to functions of state bar council under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: functions of state bar council under Advocates Act

title: Senior Advocates
definition: Section 16 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Senior Advocates".
simplifiedExplanation: High Court or Supreme Court can designate an advocate as 'Senior Advocate' based on ability, standing at the bar, or special knowledge. Senior Advocates cannot appear without a junior advocate's brief. They cannot file vakalatnama directly.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to senior advocates under the Advocates Act.

title: Right to Enrolment as Advocate
definition: Section 24 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Right to Enrolment as Advocate".
simplifiedExplanation: Any Indian citizen who has completed a law degree from a recognized university and passed the All India Bar Examination (AIBE) can enrol as an advocate in any State Bar Council. Non-citizens cannot practise law in India.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to right to enrolment as advocate under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: right to enrolment as advocate under Advocates Act

title: Advocate's Right to Practice
definition: Section 29 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Advocate's Right to Practice".
simplifiedExplanation: Every advocate enrolled with a State Bar Council has the right to practice in all courts and before all tribunals and authorities in India. There is no restriction based on state — you can practice anywhere.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to advocate's right to practice under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: advocate's right to practice under Advocates Act

title: Professional Misconduct — Disciplinary Proceedings
definition: Section 33 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Professional Misconduct — Disciplinary Proceedings".
simplifiedExplanation: If an advocate is found guilty of professional misconduct by the Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council, they can be: (1) reprimanded, (2) suspended from practice, (3) removed from roll of advocates (permanent disbarment).
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to professional misconduct — disciplinary proceedings under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: professional misconduct — disciplinary proceedings under Advocates Act

title: Punishment for Professional Misconduct
definition: Section 35 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Punishment for Professional Misconduct".
simplifiedExplanation: Disciplinary Committee can: (1) dismiss complaint, (2) reprimand advocate, (3) suspend for specified period, (4) remove name from roll. Appeal from State Bar Council Disciplinary Committee lies to BCI Disciplinary Committee.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to punishment for professional misconduct under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: punishment for professional misconduct under Advocates Act

title: Attorney General of India
definition: Section 36 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Attorney General of India".
simplifiedExplanation: Attorney General (AG) is appointed by the President under Article 76. AG is the chief law officer of India — advises the government, appears in Supreme Court on behalf of government, enjoys right of audience in all courts.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to attorney general of india under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: attorney general of india under Advocates Act

title: Advocate General of State
definition: Section 37 of the Advocates Act 1961 deals with "Advocate General of State".
simplifiedExplanation: Advocate General is appointed by the Governor under Article 165. Chief law officer of the state. Advises state government, appears in High Court for the state. Enjoys right of audience in all courts in India.
whoItAppliesTo: All advocates, law students, Bar Councils
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to advocate general of state under the Advocates Act.
scenarioTags: advocate general of state under Advocates Act

title: NALSA — National Legal Services Authority
definition: Section 3 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "NALSA — National Legal Services Authority".
simplifiedExplanation: NALSA is headed by CJI (Patron-in-Chief) and a sitting SC judge (Executive Chairman). It oversees the entire legal services system — from Supreme Court Legal Services Committee down to Taluk Legal Services Committees.
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to nalsa — national legal services authority under the LSA Act.
scenarioTags: nalsa — national legal services authority under LSA Act

title: SLSA — State Legal Services Authority
definition: Section 6 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "SLSA — State Legal Services Authority".
simplifiedExplanation: SLSA in every state headed by the Chief Justice of the High Court (Patron-in-Chief) and a sitting HC judge. Coordinates legal aid activities within the state.
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to slsa — state legal services authority under the LSA Act.
scenarioTags: slsa — state legal services authority under LSA Act

title: DLSA — District Legal Services Authority
definition: Section 9 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "DLSA — District Legal Services Authority".
simplifiedExplanation: DLSA in every district headed by the District Judge. Provides free legal aid, organizes Lok Adalats, and conducts legal awareness programs at the district level. Most legal aid applications go through DLSA.
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to dlsa — district legal services authority under the LSA Act.
scenarioTags: dlsa — district legal services authority under LSA Act

title: Who Is Entitled to Free Legal Aid
definition: Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "Who Is Entitled to Free Legal Aid".
simplifiedExplanation: Free legal aid for: (1) SC/ST members, (2) women and children, (3) persons with disabilities, (4) industrial workers, (5) persons in custody, (6) victims of mass disaster, trafficking, or ethnic violence, (7) persons earning less than ₹3 lakh/year (₹5 lakh in SC).
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to who is entitled to free legal aid under the LSA Act.

scenarioTags: who is entitled to free legal aid under LSA Act

title: Lok Adalat — Constitution
definition: Section 19 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "Lok Adalat — Constitution".
simplifiedExplanation: NALSA/SLSA/DLSA can organize Lok Adalats at every level. Lok Adalat can settle: (1) cases pending in courts, (2) matters at pre-litigation stage. Award is binding and final. No appeal. No court fee.
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to lok adalat — constitution under the LSA Act.
scenarioTags: lok adalat — constitution under LSA Act

title: Permanent Lok Adalat for Public Utility Services
definition: Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 deals with "Permanent Lok Adalat for Public Utility Services".
simplifiedExplanation: Permanent Lok Adalat for: electricity, transport, postal services, insurance, telecom. Can deal with disputes up to ₹1 crore. Unlike regular Lok Adalat, it can decide even without consent of both parties.
whoItAppliesTo: Economically weaker sections, SC/ST, women, children, disabled, and other eligible persons
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to permanent lok adalat for public utility services under the LSA Act.

scenarioTags: permanent lok adalat for public utility services under LSA Act

title: Extradition Treaty
definition: Section 2(d) of the Extradition Act 1962 deals with "Extradition Treaty".
simplifiedExplanation: India has extradition treaties with about 48 countries and extradition arrangements with about 12 countries. Treaty specifies which offences are extraditable, procedures, and safeguards.
whoItAppliesTo: Fugitive criminals, foreign governments seeking extradition from India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to extradition treaty under the Extradition Act.

title: Extradition of Fugitive Criminal
definition: Section 3 of the Extradition Act 1962 deals with "Extradition of Fugitive Criminal".
simplifiedExplanation: A fugitive criminal (person accused or convicted in a foreign country who is found in India) may be extradited to the requesting country. Dual criminality required: the offence must be a crime in both countries.
whoItAppliesTo: Fugitive criminals, foreign governments seeking extradition from India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to extradition of fugitive criminal under the Extradition Act.
scenarioTags: extradition of fugitive criminal under Extradition Act

title: Restrictions on Surrender
definition: Section 8 of the Extradition Act 1962 deals with "Restrictions on Surrender".
simplifiedExplanation: Extradition refused if: (1) offence is political, (2) prosecution is for political reasons, (3) offence is trivial, (4) request is not in good faith, (5) person might be prejudiced due to race/religion/nationality, (6) statute of limitations expired.
whoItAppliesTo: Fugitive criminals, foreign governments seeking extradition from India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to restrictions on surrender under the Extradition Act.
scenarioTags: restrictions on surrender under Extradition Act

title: Surrender of Fugitive Criminal by India
definition: Section 21 of the Extradition Act 1962 deals with "Surrender of Fugitive Criminal by India".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can surrender a fugitive criminal to the requesting state after judicial process confirms the extradition request is valid. The person can challenge extradition in High Court and Supreme Court.
whoItAppliesTo: Fugitive criminals, foreign governments seeking extradition from India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to surrender of fugitive criminal by india under the Extradition Act.
tags: surrender of fugitive criminal by india
aiSearchKeywords: surrender of fugitive criminal by india
scenarioTags: surrender of fugitive criminal by india under Extradition Act

title: Application for Extradition by India
definition: Section 34B of the Extradition Act 1962 deals with "Application for Extradition by India".
simplifiedExplanation: When India wants a criminal extradited from another country, the request goes through the Ministry of External Affairs via diplomatic channels. India has requested extradition in several high-profile cases.
whoItAppliesTo: Fugitive criminals, foreign governments seeking extradition from India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to application for extradition by india under the Extradition Act.

title: Prohibition to Accept Foreign Contribution
definition: Section 3 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "Prohibition to Accept Foreign Contribution".
simplifiedExplanation: The following CANNOT accept foreign contribution: (1) election candidates, (2) journalists/media, (3) judges, (4) government servants, (5) members of legislature, (6) political parties, (7) organizations of political nature.
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to prohibition to accept foreign contribution under the FCRA.
scenarioTags: prohibition to accept foreign contribution under FCRA

title: FCRA Registration Required
definition: Section 6 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "FCRA Registration Required".
simplifiedExplanation: Any person wanting to accept foreign contribution must be registered under FCRA or obtain prior permission. Registration is valid for 5 years (reduced from permanent after 2020 amendment). Must use a designated SBI bank account.
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to fcra registration required under the FCRA.

title: Restriction on Use of Foreign Contribution
definition: Section 8 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "Restriction on Use of Foreign Contribution".
simplifiedExplanation: Foreign contribution must be used ONLY for the purpose for which registration was granted. Cannot be used for speculative activities. After 2020 amendment: not more than 20% can be used for administrative expenses.
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to restriction on use of foreign contribution under the FCRA.
tags: restriction on use of foreign contribution
aiSearchKeywords: restriction on use of foreign contribution
scenarioTags: restriction on use of foreign contribution under FCRA

title: Suspension or Cancellation of Registration
definition: Section 11 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "Suspension or Cancellation of Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can suspend FCRA registration for 180 days (pending inquiry) or cancel it permanently if: (1) false statements made, (2) funds used for unauthorized purpose, (3) not in public interest. Over 6,000 NGO registrations cancelled recently.
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to suspension or cancellation of registration under the FCRA.
scenarioTags: suspension or cancellation of registration under FCRA

title: Cancellation of Certificate of Registration
definition: Section 14 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "Cancellation of Certificate of Registration".
simplifiedExplanation: Certificate cancelled if: NGO has not used foreign contribution reasonably, violated provisions of the Act, or engaged in activities detrimental to national interest. Cancellation means NGO cannot receive any foreign funds.
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to cancellation of certificate of registration under the FCRA.
scenarioTags: cancellation of certificate of registration under FCRA

title: Penalty for Violation
definition: Section 35 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 deals with "Penalty for Violation".
simplifiedExplanation: Receiving foreign contribution without registration, violating conditions of registration, not filing annual returns — all punishable.
punishment: Up to 5 years imprisonment or fine or both. Accepting foreign contribution without registration: up to 5 years + fine
whoItAppliesTo: NGOs, associations, individuals receiving foreign contributions
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalty for violation under the FCRA.

title: Passport or Travel Document Required for Departure
definition: Section 3 of the Passports Act 1967 deals with "Passport or Travel Document Required for Departure".
simplifiedExplanation: No person shall depart from or attempt to depart from India unless they hold a valid passport or travel document. Leaving India without passport: criminal offence.
punishment: Up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to ₹500 or both
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens, persons entering/leaving India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to passport or travel document required for departure under the Passports Act.
tags: passport or travel document required for departure
aiSearchKeywords: passport or travel document required for departure
scenarioTags: passport or travel document required for departure under Passports Act

title: Applications for Passports
definition: Section 5 of the Passports Act 1967 deals with "Applications for Passports".
simplifiedExplanation: Any Indian citizen can apply for a passport to the Passport Authority. Passport Seva Kendras handle applications. Normal processing: 30 days. Tatkaal (urgent): 1-3 days with additional fee.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens, persons entering/leaving India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to applications for passports under the Passports Act.
scenarioTags: applications for passports under Passports Act

title: Refusal of Passport
definition: Section 6 of the Passports Act 1967 deals with "Refusal of Passport".
simplifiedExplanation: Passport can be refused if: (1) applicant is not an Indian citizen, (2) proceedings pending before court, (3) warrant/summons outstanding, (4) departure prohibited by any court, (5) security reasons, (6) convicted for moral turpitude (last 2 years).
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens, persons entering/leaving India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to refusal of passport under the Passports Act.
scenarioTags: refusal of passport under Passports Act

title: Variation, Impounding and Revocation
definition: Section 10 of the Passports Act 1967 deals with "Variation, Impounding and Revocation".
simplifiedExplanation: Passport Authority can: (1) vary conditions, (2) impound passport, (3) revoke passport. Common reason for impounding: pending criminal cases. Passport revocation used in cases of Mallya, Nirav Modi.
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens, persons entering/leaving India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to variation, impounding and revocation under the Passports Act.
scenarioTags: variation, impounding and revocation under Passports Act

title: Offences and Penalties
definition: Section 12 of the Passports Act 1967 deals with "Offences and Penalties".
simplifiedExplanation: Offences: furnishing false information, tampering with passport, using passport of another, possessing multiple passports.
punishment: Up to 2 years imprisonment or fine up to ₹5,000 or both. Fraudulent passport: up to 5 years + fine up to ₹10,000
whoItAppliesTo: All Indian citizens, persons entering/leaving India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to offences and penalties under the Passports Act.
scenarioTags: offences and penalties under Passports Act

title: Foreigner Defined
definition: Section 2(a) of the Foreigners Act 1946 deals with "Foreigner Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: A foreigner is any person who is not a citizen of India. Even persons of Indian origin holding foreign passports are foreigners. The burden of proof is on the person to prove they are NOT a foreigner.
whoItAppliesTo: All foreign nationals in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to foreigner defined under the Foreigners Act.

title: Power to Make Orders Against Foreigners
definition: Section 3 of the Foreigners Act 1946 deals with "Power to Make Orders Against Foreigners".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can make orders regarding: (1) prohibiting entry, (2) restricting movement, (3) requiring residence at specific place, (4) requiring registration, (5) deportation. Very wide powers.
whoItAppliesTo: All foreign nationals in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to power to make orders against foreigners under the Foreigners Act.
tags: power to make orders against foreigners
aiSearchKeywords: power to make orders against foreigners
scenarioTags: power to make orders against foreigners under Foreigners Act

title: Burden of Proof
definition: Section 9 of the Foreigners Act 1946 deals with "Burden of Proof".
simplifiedExplanation: If any question arises whether a person is or is not a foreigner, the burden of proof is on THAT PERSON — not the government. This is a reverse burden and has been controversial especially in Assam NRC context.
whoItAppliesTo: All foreign nationals in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to burden of proof under the Foreigners Act.
scenarioTags: burden of proof under Foreigners Act

title: Penalties
definition: Section 14 of the Foreigners Act 1946 deals with "Penalties".
simplifiedExplanation: Foreigners who violate any order or overstay their visa period are punishable. Illegal entry into India: up to 5 years imprisonment. Harbouring illegal foreigners is also punishable.
whoItAppliesTo: All foreign nationals in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to penalties under the Foreigners Act.

title: Deportation of Foreigners
definition: Section 3(2)(c) of the Foreigners Act 1946 deals with "Deportation of Foreigners".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can deport any foreigner from India. The deportation order is not subject to ordinary judicial review. Foreigners Tribunals in Assam determine whether a person is a foreigner for NRC purposes.
whoItAppliesTo: All foreign nationals in India
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to deportation of foreigners under the Foreigners Act.
scenarioTags: deportation of foreigners under Foreigners Act

title: Fast-Track Citizenship for Persecuted Minorities
definition: Section 2 (Amendment to Citizenship Act) of the Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 deals with "Fast-Track Citizenship for Persecuted Minorities".
simplifiedExplanation: Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who entered India before December 31, 2014 are eligible for Indian citizenship. Residency requirement reduced from 11 years to 5 years.
whoItAppliesTo: Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to fast-track citizenship for persecuted minorities under the CAA.
scenarioTags: fast-track citizenship for persecuted minorities under CAA

title: Citizenship by Registration or Naturalisation
definition: Section 3 (New Section 6B) of the Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 deals with "Citizenship by Registration or Naturalisation".
simplifiedExplanation: Persons of the 6 specified religions from the 3 specified countries are deemed to have been granted citizenship from the date of their entry into India. They cannot be treated as illegal migrants or prosecuted for entering without documents.
whoItAppliesTo: Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to citizenship by registration or naturalisation under the CAA.
scenarioTags: citizenship by registration or naturalisation under CAA

title: Areas Where CAA Does Not Apply
definition: Section 6 (Exceptions) of the Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 deals with "Areas Where CAA Does Not Apply".
simplifiedExplanation: CAA does NOT apply to tribal areas of: Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura (protected under 6th Schedule) and areas with Inner Line Permit (Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram). This was done to address NE concerns.
whoItAppliesTo: Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to areas where caa does not apply under the CAA.

scenarioTags: areas where caa does not apply under CAA

title: Constitutional Challenge to CAA
definition: Controversy of the Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 deals with "Constitutional Challenge to CAA".
simplifiedExplanation: CAA is challenged on grounds of: (1) violates Article 14 — classifying migrants based on religion, (2) violates secular character of Constitution, (3) discriminates against Muslims. Supreme Court has not yet decided. 200+ petitions pending.
whoItAppliesTo: Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to constitutional challenge to caa under the CAA.
scenarioTags: constitutional challenge to caa under CAA

title: Essential Commodities Defined
definition: Section 2A of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Essential Commodities Defined".
simplifiedExplanation: Essential commodities include: foodstuffs (cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar), drugs, fertilizers, petroleum products, seeds, and any commodity notified by government. The list can be expanded during emergencies.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, manufacturers, dealers of essential commodities
realWorldExample: This section is commonly invoked in matters related to essential commodities defined under the EC Act.

title: Powers to Control Production, Supply, Distribution
definition: Section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Powers to Control Production, Supply, Distribution".
simplifiedExplanation: Central Government can regulate: (1) production, (2) supply, (3) distribution, (4) pricing of essential commodities. Can impose stock limits, regulate trade, fix prices. Most powerful provision for controlling black marketing.

title: Stock Limits on Dealers
definition: Section 3(2)(c) of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Stock Limits on Dealers".
simplifiedExplanation: Government can impose maximum stock limits on dealers and retailers. Hoarding (keeping more than permitted stock) is punishable. This prevents artificial scarcity and price rises.

title: Confiscation of Essential Commodities (2020 Amendment)
definition: Section 6A of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Confiscation of Essential Commodities (2020 Amendment)".
simplifiedExplanation: After 2020 amendment, stock limits can be imposed on agricultural produce ONLY if: (1) retail price rises 100% for horticultural produce, (2) retail price rises 50% for non-perishable agricultural produce. This was part of agricultural reforms.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, manufacturers, dealers of essential commodities

title: Penalties for Contravention
definition: Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Penalties for Contravention".
simplifiedExplanation: Hoarding essential commodities, violating price control orders, or black marketing is punishable with up to 7 years imprisonment. Repeat offenders face enhanced punishment.
punishment: Up to 7 years imprisonment + fine. For adulterated/misbranded food: up to life imprisonment
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, manufacturers, dealers of essential commodities

title: Power to Search and Seize
definition: Section 10 of the Essential Commodities Act 1955 deals with "Power to Search and Seize".
simplifiedExplanation: Any police officer or authorized person can enter, search premises, and seize essential commodities being hoarded or sold illegally. Seized goods can be confiscated and sold at fair price.
whoItAppliesTo: Producers, manufacturers, dealers of essential commodities

title: Certification Agency

title: Seed Testing Laboratories
definition: Section 7 of the Seeds Act 1966 deals with "Seed Testing Laboratories".
simplifiedExplanation: Central and State Seed Testing Laboratories test seed samples for quality. Any person can get their seeds tested. Lab results are accepted as evidence in court.

title: Minimum Standards — Seed Analyst

title: Penalty for Selling Misbranded Seeds

simplifiedExplanation: Selling seeds with false labels (wrong variety, wrong quality parameters, wrong manufacturer name) is punishable.

definition: Source 5 of the Sources of Indian Law deals with "Presidential Ordinances (Article 123)".

title: Judicial Precedents — Stare Decisis
definition: Source 6 of the Sources of Indian Law deals with "Judicial Precedents — Stare Decisis".
simplifiedExplanation: Law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on ALL courts in India (Article 141). High Court decisions bind all courts within their state. This is the doctrine of stare decisis — courts must follow earlier decisions of superior courts.

simplifiedExplanation: Unwritten customs and conventions are recognized as sources of law. Personal laws (Hindu, Muslim) are based on customs. Constitutional conventions (PM must be from majority party) are not enforceable in court but are followed.

simplifiedExplanation: Treaties ratified by India become part of Indian law when Parliament enacts implementing legislation. Some treaties are directly enforceable (self-executing), others need domestic legislation. Article 253 gives Parliament power to make laws implementing treaties.
